# PREFACE.

### I.

-> O Leonardo, why do you labor so much? <note>original: "perchè tanto penate?" This is a famous rhetorical question found in Leonardo’s own notebooks, where he often reflected on his relentless drive for knowledge and perfection.</note> <-
-> *Atlantic Codex, f. 71 r.* <note>The Atlantic Codex (Codice Atlantico) is the largest collection of Leonardo da Vinci's drawings and writings, currently preserved in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan.</note> <-

Leonardo’s biography, in its essential outlines, is the history of the birth, the growth, the magnification, and the expansion of an intellectual love for nature—a love intent on reproducing her forms and understanding her laws. This love, born in a humble house in Anchiano <note>Anchiano is a small hamlet near the town of Vinci, traditionally identified as Leonardo's birthplace.</note> shortly after 1452, broadened through a progressive development to embrace nature within the infinity of space, time, and form.

L. DA VINCI.

# PREFACE.

The first memory that Leonardo preserves for us in his manuscripts, among the fragments concerning his childhood, seems almost like a prophecy: *In the first recollection of my childhood*, he writes, recalling a vision from his youth, *it seemed to me that, while I was in my cradle, a kite <note>A "nibbio" is a bird of prey in the hawk family. This specific memory became famous in later centuries, particularly through Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic interpretation of Leonardo's life.</note> came to me, opened my mouth with its tail, and struck me many times with that tail inside my lips.* (Atlantic Codex, f. 161 r.) A Greek tradition tells that bees announced to the world that Demosthenes <note>Demosthenes (384–322 BC) was the most celebrated orator of ancient Greece; legend says bees settled on his lips as a child, symbolizing his future eloquence.</note> would be the sweetest and most exquisite political orator; does the kite not seem here to foreshadow the most elevated and clear describer of nature? Leonardo himself is gripped by this superstitious thought: his life must be the fulfillment of the arduous task of revealing nature's secrets to mankind. Beside the preceding lines, he writes this revealing expression: *it seems it is my destiny.* <note>original: "par che sia mio destino."</note>

At the dawn of his life as an artist, around 1472, Leonardo's pursuit was to revive in his own imagination the figure

> ...desire, eager to see the great mingling of the various and strange forms made by artful nature <note>original: "artifiziosa natura." In the Renaissance, "artful" or "artificial" meant something crafted with great skill or ingenuity, rather than something "fake."</note>, having wandered for some time among the shadowy rocks, I arrived at the entrance of a great cavern; before which—standing for a moment struck with amazement and ignorance of such a thing—having bent my back into an arch, and resting my tired hand upon my knee, with my right hand I shaded my lowered and closed eyelids. And frequently bending this way and that to see if I could discern anything within, though this was denied to me by the intense darkness that was there; and after I had stayed a while, suddenly two things were awakened within me: fear and desire; fear of the menacing dark cave, and desire to see if there were any miraculous thing within. » (*R.*, § 1339.)

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nature is the great mystery that Leonardo seeks to investigate.

tellect leads him to scientific investigation. Through a slow progression, Leonardo is led back from the *Last Supper* <note>Original: *Cenacolo*. Leonardo’s famous mural in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan.</note> to that *Treatise on Light and Shadow*, to which he had already dedicated his first efforts in Florence; from the Sforza Monument <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive bronze equestrian statue intended to honor Francesco Sforza, which was never cast.</note> to the *Treatise on the anatomy of the horse and on the methods of bronze casting*; from various works of military and civil architecture to the *Treatise on weights and motions* and to that of *Hydraulics.*\* The anecdote itself, narrated by Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the biographer whose "Lives of the Artists" is a primary source for Renaissance art history.</note> regarding the *Last Supper*, is an echo of the contrasts that his essentially speculative way of living aroused at this time. Before 1499, the practitioner has by now disappeared in Da Vinci; he places the brush in the hands of his disciples; abandoning the circle of artists, he positions himself in the very midst of the Milanese scientists, by now driven by a single goal: to solve the infinite problems that nature presented to him incessantly.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page XII regarding Leonardo’s transition from an active artist to a theoretical scientist, contrasting his intellectual needs with the practical demands of the 15th century.</meta>

<page-num>XIII</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

The 15th century was hostile to this transition: driven by the thirst for a renewal, it demanded not thought, but action <note>Original: *fare*, literally "to do" or "to make." The author contrasts the Renaissance's focus on tangible creation with Leonardo's desire for theoretical understanding.</note>. Leonardo, on the other hand, was born for the labor of thought. Poetry, painting, sculpture, architecture, music, the inventions of printing, gunpowder, and mechanical instruments, and geographical discoveries—at their most marvelous peak—were what the Renaissance saw and admired: abstract law <note>The underlying scientific principles or mathematical logic governing the physical world.</note> was not appreciated for its true value; its inherent logic was almost not understood. Leonardo, however, driven by an overwhelming need, moves from the concrete to the abstract, from practice to theory, and from art to science, developing that same spiritual tendency which, though born around him, was only to manifest fully two centuries later <note>A reference to the formalization of the scientific method during the 17th-century Enlightenment.</note>.

In 1500, the character of Da Vinci's life is clearly defined: his dominant idea is to develop and bring his natural research to completion; his firm resolve is to make as few concessions as possible to the spirit of the age.

It argues that Leonardo's shift toward abstract theory and natural philosophy anticipated the scientific developments of the 17th century.</summary>

<page-num>XIV</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

In 1502, while serving as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia <note>The ambitious and often ruthless son of Pope Alexander VI; he employed Leonardo to design fortifications and maps.</note>, he felt that the constraints of practical work were stripping away his broad theoretical visions: he then withdrew to Florence. In 1501, he had received urgent requests from Isabella d’Este <note>The Marchioness of Mantua and a preeminent patron of the Renaissance.</note>, through the General of the Carmelites, Pietro da Nuvolaria, "so that he might make a small painting of the Madonna, devout and sweet, as is his natural style." Da Vinci had promised warmly, and then, lost in scientific investigations, had done nothing about it. "As far as I can tell," the friar had replied to the noble Marchioness of Mantua, "Leonardo’s life is so varied and highly unsettled that he seems to live from day to day. Since arriving in Florence, he has only produced a sketch of a cartoon <note>original: "schizo d'uno cartone." A cartoon is a full-scale preparatory drawing for a painting.</note>, in which he depicts a Christ child about one year old. He has done nothing else, except that two of his assistants are painting portraits, and he occasionally lends a hand to one of them. **HE IS DEVOTING HIMSELF INTENSELY TO GEOMETRY, AND IS EXTREMELY IMPATIENT WITH THE BRUSH.**" Now, on May 13, 1504, after a futile wait, Isabella returned to the pursuit, asking him by letter

On May 27, fourteen days later, an agent, Angelo del Tovaglia, replied to her: "He has promised me many times to do it during certain hours and times that remain over from a work undertaken here for this Signory <note>The *Signoria* was the governing body of the Republic of Florence; the work referred to is the *Battle of Anghiari*.</note>. I shall not fail to urge both this Leonardo and also Perugino regarding that other [commission]; both promise me well, and seem to have a great desire to serve Your Excellency. However <note>original Latin: "Tamen"</note>, I strongly doubt they will not end up competing in a race of tardiness <note>original: "gara de tarditate." A witty remark on the notorious reputation both artists had for delaying or never finishing projects.</note>: I do not know who will overcome the other in this: **I HOLD IT FOR CERTAIN THAT LEONARDO WILL BE THE WINNER.**" Pietro Perugino promptly fulfilled his commitment; Leonardo was then undertaking the painting of the *Battle of Anghiari*, driven by necessity and the pleas of the Florentines.

<page-num>XVI</page-num>

### PREFACE

In 1506 Alessandro Amadori, Leonardo’s uncle, took to heart the desire of the Marchioness d’Este, and secured a promise from his nephew for the completion of a small, soft, and sweet painting: “And he has completely promised me he will shortly begin the work to satisfy your ladyship’s desire, to whose grace he much recommends himself.” <note>Original Italian: "Et lui al tutto me ha promesso comincerà in breve l’ opera per satisfare al desiderio di V. S., alla cui gratia assai si raccomanda."</note> Isabella replied with a few discouraged lines; then she fell silent forever. Time passed, and Leonardo did nothing, forgetful of both his promise and his brush. As if to compensate for Leonardo’s stubbornness, his pupil Salai, in those very days, showed a “great desire to do something gallant for the Marchioness.” <note>Salai, born Gian Giacomo Caprotti, was Leonardo’s favorite pupil and frequent model, though he was often described by the master as "a glutton, a thief, and stubborn."</note> His offer was not accepted.*

Meanwhile, the *Battle of Anghiari*, which he had begun to draw with such care and enthusiasm, was abandoned at the first stages, in the same way as the preparatory drawing of *Adam and Eve*, the *Head of Medusa*, and the *Adoration of the Magi*, “as happened in almost all his affairs.” <note>Leonardo was famous for his "non-finito" (unfinished) works, often losing interest in a project once he had solved the technical or artistic challenges it presented.</note>

<page-num>XVII</page-num>

# PREFACE

What was the cause of this reluctance to paint? Why was it that Leonardo did not satisfy the requests of a refined princess, nor the general expectations of his native city? A few dates will provide a clear answer. The *Codex on the Flight of Birds* <note>Original Italian: *Codice sul volo degli uccelli*. This notebook, now in Turin, contains Leonardo’s most advanced theories on aerodynamics and his designs for a flying machine.</note> dates back to 1504 (V. U., 5 r.); <note>“V. U.” refers to *Volo degli Uccelli* (Flight of Birds), folio 5 recto.</note> his mathematical work regarding spherical sections dates to 1505. (R., § 1374.) <note>“R.” likely refers to Jean Paul Richter’s seminal 1883 compilation of Leonardo’s literary works.</note> His research into perspective, which began even before 1482; his studies of anatomy, conducted systematically since 1489; and those of mechanics, which kept him occupied before 1497, all continued in Florence after 1500. These were joined by his studies on the canalization of the Arno River, which gave birth and life to the modern principles of hydraulics and terrestrial dynamics. <note>Leonardo proposed a massive engineering project to make the Arno navigable between Florence and the sea, bypassing its more treacherous stretches.</note> On May 22, 1508, as if crowning a long period of tireless scientific activity, an idea emerged in Leonardo’s mind for a temporary general reorganization of his manuscript notes:

> “And this shall be a collection without order,” he writes as he begins the *British Museum Codex*, <note>Now known as the Codex Arundel, held by the British Library. It is a dense collection of notes on various subjects including physics and geometry.</note> “drawn from...”

<summary>This page explains that Leonardo's "intolerance" for painting was caused by his deep immersion in scientific research, including anatomy, mechanics, and the canalization of the Arno. It marks the moment in 1508 when he began attempting to organize his vast, chaotic collection of notes.</summary>

# PREFACE

...many papers, which I have copied here, hoping later to put them in order in their proper places, according to the subjects they will deal with.” (*R.*, 4.) <note>Original: "molte carte, le quali io ho qui copiate..." This continues Leonardo’s introductory note to the Codex Arundel, where he admits his notes are a "collection without order" drawn from many papers he had already written.</note>

This impatience toward "productive art" <note>The author uses "productive art" (*arte produttrice*) to refer to the physical creation of paintings and sculptures for clients, as opposed to the theoretical study of nature.</note> began as soon as the empirical practice of painting was superseded by the
<margin>|</margin>
concept that to create, one must know the forms and the laws of phenomena. This attitude became harmful in Florence after 1472; <note>1472 marks the year Leonardo was recorded as a master in the Guild of St. Luke in Florence, beginning his professional career.</note> it was forgotten for a moment in Milan after 1482; <note>The year Leonardo moved to Milan to serve Ludovico Sforza, where he was initially more prolific in his artistic output.</note> it reasserted itself with greater violence after 1494; <note>The year of the French invasion of Italy and the beginning of the Italian Wars, which disrupted many of Leonardo's projects, including the great bronze horse.</note> it became a necessity at the opening of the new 16th century; and it continued amidst ever-weakening resistance until his death. To his contemporaries, this seemed like a crime. They knew no other form of activity than that which was practical and artistic: science had taken refuge in the cloisters and was called theology; or it had lost itself in the inner chambers of the Kabbalah and was called magic. <note>The author highlights that Leonardo’s empirical, observational "science" was unrecognizable to a society that viewed intellectual pursuit only through the lens of religion or the occult.</note>

He set out alongside Perugino and Credi, and with Bramante and Sangallo <note>Pietro Perugino and Lorenzo di Credi were fellow pupils of Leonardo in Verrocchio's workshop; Donato Bramante and the Sangallo family were the preeminent architects of the age.</note> upon the fertile path of practical application, yet, in his solitude, he lost himself in science; the necessities of life and the spirit of the age induced him to grasp at art for a brief moment, but the depths of his mind dragged him back once more to theoretical and abstract investigation. The story of his life is the repetition of this perpetual cycle, which fractured and undermined his work and his influence: it was not the serene life of tradition, but the shipwreck of an entire being, who yearned for what his century forbade him, and who desired what his century denied him.

Viewed in this light, Leonardo da Vinci appears in his true historical perspective: the "highly varied and indeterminate" <note>Original: "vario et indeterminato forte." This contemporary description of Leonardo's character highlights how his peers struggled to categorize his multifaceted and often unfinished work.</note> character of his existence is understood through his...

[A deep] sorrow clouded Leonardo’s soul in these final days; his life had been a restless search for natural laws, but the conflict with time had broken his spirit and condemned his work to remain unfinished. Surrounded by his disciples and men of the cloth, da Vinci sought to renew within his spirit the simple faith of his childhood, but death took him on May 2, 1519.

The primary concern of his will had been to leave to Master Francesco Melzi, a gentleman of Milan, “as remuneration for the services, pleasing to him, performed in the past, each and every book that the said testator currently possesses.” <note>Original Italian: "per remuneratione de' servitii, ad epso grati, a lui facti per il passato, tutti et ciaschaduno li libri, che il dicto testatore ha de presente." <page-num>XXXIV</page-num>

<header>### PREFACE</header>

...and the allegories, the prophecies, and the witticisms, before assuming that admirably literary form in which they are preserved for us, delighted the refined conversations of the 15th-century Milanese Court.

Leonardo was an elegant speaker because the sweet Tuscan idiom <note>The dialect of Florence, which was considered the most prestigious and "correct" form of Italian during the Renaissance.</note> sounded from his lips; he was also so by the nature of his delicate and sincere soul, full at times of vivacity, charm, and grace.

Vinci the speaker is reflected in Vinci the writer, with the addition of that powerful reflection which, penetrating into the heart of man and into the secrets of the natural world, captured the deepest reasons for the good, the true, and the beautiful. The idea that Leonardo is a careless writer, due to the spontaneity and perceived roughness of his speech, must henceforth be dismissed.

Leonardo’s supreme goal is the greatest clarity within the greatest conciseness; that redundant and rhythmic <note>The original Italian *numeroso* refers to a traditional, flowery style of prose that followed specific rhythmic patterns or "numbers" inherited from Latin rhetoric.</note> way of writing—the primary enemy of pure thought—which was born with the stories of Boccaccio... <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), famous for the *Decameron*; his complex, winding sentence structures became the standard for Italian prose, a style Leonardo consciously avoided in favor of directness.</note>

The manuscripts are full of erasures, and every crossing-out cleanses away a slight obscurity that veils the understanding of the concept: the language, shaped into style, is the clear glass through which the thought unfolds with clarity. The definition of <term>Perspective</term> <note>The mathematical and artistic system for representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface.</note> is repeated by Leonardo more than ten times with an incessant changing of its "outer layers," in order to clothe it in the most evident and simplest form (MS A, f. 3 r. 10 v.); a letter to Giuliano de' Medici is written and rewritten with continuous <term>revisions</term> <note>original: *pentimenti*. This term usually refers to an artist changing their mind during a painting, leaving traces of the previous work beneath the surface.</note>, so that the thought might align with its expression with the greatest identity of sign and meaning (Codex Atlanticus, 278 r.). ...most admirable figure, in order to express in a painting his own exalted image, just so in the sweet <term>Tuscan idiom</term> <note>The dialect of Tuscany, which became the foundation for the modern Italian language; Leonardo viewed it as a living, flexible tool.</note>, which he possessed in all its variety and vividness, he sought out the words suited to the high meaning that his spirit—an interpreter of nature—suggested to him. <term>Leonardo da Vinci</term> is also an artist of language: his literary work, compared to the redundant prose of the idle imitators of the ancients <note>Referring to the "Humanists" of the Renaissance who often wrote in a stiff, overly-formal style imitating classical Latin authors.</note>, has the same effect as a ray of sunlight on a countryside oppressed by a dark cloud—a ray that heralds a new awakening of life.

Clarity is obtained only through the precision of terms, just as conciseness is not possible without precision of thought. This precision of language was sought by Leonardo in a series of studies preserved for us in his manuscripts; the precision of thought is a result of his very nature, which was an enemy to anything indeterminate or vague.

The inaccurate transcription of the manuscripts required a continuous comparison with the <term>heliotype</term> <note>An early photographic process used to create high-quality reproductions of documents and images.</note> reproduction of the <term>codices</term> <note>Handwritten books or collections of manuscript pages, as opposed to printed volumes.</note> or with the originals themselves. The absence of natural word division and of any punctuation marks necessitated a laborious preliminary interpretation.

No less difficulty was presented by the selection: the intent to eliminate every fragment of a purely scientific nature, to leave space only for the expression of broad and easily intelligible ideas, demanded constant discernment.

In the original disorder of the manuscripts, which forces the reader's mind to jump between the most disparate ideas, it was also impossible to find a common thread that could provide a rule for the organization of the selection. It was therefore necessary to search within the content of the individual fragments themselves for a criterion of order, so that each concept would be linked to the next through a kind of logical progression, from which a sense [would derive]...

The purely literary works, gathered from their original scattered state and already distinguishable by their very character into several well-defined groups, were arranged by me according to what would presumably have been Da Vinci’s own concept. Leonardo’s *Fables*, prepared by centuries of development during the Middle Ages, expand their scope from the animal world to the vegetable and inorganic. The *Allegories*, which as a whole form a veritable *Bestiary* <note>A collection of short descriptions about all sorts of animals, real and imaginary, intended to teach a spiritual or moral lesson.</note>, although mostly not original, preserve the traces of a new development worthy of appreciation. The *Descriptions and Portraits*, where the literary purpose is combined with the pictorial; the *Prophecies and Witticisms* <note>original: "Facezie" — short, humorous stories or clever remarks intended to amuse or satirize.</note>, where the sharp wit of a researcher is revealed alongside that of a man of the world, complete the cycle of purely artistic works.

<page-num>XLII</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

A difficult question had to be addressed alongside the development of the collection of fragments, and that is the question of their originality. The *Notes*, which follow the selection step-by-step and can be found at the end of the volume, indicate the source from which <term>Leonardo</term> <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), though known as a lone genius, often took notes from classical and medieval authors to study or critique their ideas.</note> drew this or that fragment; however, the broader question of the originality of his work in all its parts is addressed by me in a <term>monograph</term> <note>A detailed, specialized study on a single subject.</note> titled *On the sources of Leonardo da Vinci's literary and scientific work* <note>original: "Intorno alle fonti dell' opera letteraria e scientifica di Leonardo da Vinci"</note>, which will be published as soon as possible.

Finally, I must point out that the small footnotes at the bottom of the page have no other purpose than to make the understanding of <term>Leonardo’s text</term> <note>original: "testo leonardiano"</note> easier for the reader and to remove any doubts that might obscure the meaning of the expressions.

The references to the works that served as the basis for this collection have been made for each fragment in the SUMMARIES and REFERENCES, using appropriate abbreviations.

### I. — RESTLESSNESS.

The torrent carried so much earth and stones into its bed that it was forced to change its location. <note>Leonardo often used natural phenomena, like the shifting of a riverbed, to illustrate the unintended consequences of chaotic movement or "restlessness."</note>

### II. — THE PAPER AND THE INK.

Finding itself all stained by the dark blackness of the ink, the paper complains of it; to which the ink shows that, because of the words composed upon it, he is the reason for the paper's preservation. <note>This fable serves as an allegory for the value of the written word; while the ink appears to "soil" the purity of the paper, it is only through this marking that the paper is deemed worthy of being kept for posterity.</note>

### III. — THE WATER.

Finding itself in the proud sea, its own element, the water was seized by a desire to rise above the air; and, encouraged by the element of fire, having risen as a thin vapor, it seemed almost to possess the subtlety of the air. Having climbed on high, it reached the thinnest and coldest layers of the air, where it was ab— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("ab-") at the end of the page; it likely continues with "abbandonata" (abandoned) or "abbracciata" (embraced) by the cold, leading to its eventual condensation and fall as rain.</note>

### IV. — THE FLAME AND THE CANDLE.

The flames, having already lasted a month in the glass furnace <note>Leonardo frequently observed the glass-blowing furnaces of his time; they provided a constant, controlled source of intense heat compared to the fleeting life of a candle.</note>, saw a candle approaching in a beautiful and shining candlestick. With great desire, they struggled to draw near to it. One among them, leaving its natural course and drawing itself <insert>from within</insert> <note>The original Italian note "* da entro" clarifies the flame's movement through the wood.</note> a hollow firebrand <term>firebrand: a piece of burning wood or coal, often used as a source of fuel or to move a flame</term> where it was feeding, emerged through a small crack on the opposite side. It threw itself upon the nearby candle and, devouring it with extreme greed and gluttony, brought it nearly to its end. Wanting then to prolong its life, it tried in vain to return to the furnace from which it had departed; but it was forced to die and perish along with the candle. Thus, in the end, with wailing and repentance, it turned into offensive smoke, leaving all its sisters to their splendid, long lives and beauty. <note>This fable serves as a warning against leaving a secure and "natural" position out of envy or greed for something that appears more attractive but is ultimately unsustainable.</note>

## V. — THOSE WHO HUMBLE THEMSELVES,
### ARE EXALTED. <note>This title is a direct reference to the Gospel of Luke 14:11: "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted." Leonardo frequently used biblical themes to frame his observations of the natural world.</note>

A certain small amount of snow, finding itself clinging to the top of a rock which was positioned upon the extreme peak of a very high mountain, withdrew into its own imagination and began to consider within itself, saying:
— Should I not be judged haughty and proud, for having placed myself—a tiny dram <term>dram: historically a very small unit of weight; here Leonardo uses it to emphasize the snow's insignificance</term> of snow—in such a high place, and for allowing such a great quantity of snow as can be seen from here to remain lower than me? Certainly, my small quantity does not deserve this height; for I can well know, by the evidence of my small form, what the sun did yesterday to my companions, who in a few hours were undone by the sun; and this happened because they had placed themselves higher than was required of them.
I wish to flee the wrath of the sun, and lower myself, and find a place suitable for my small <gloss>small</gloss> <note>original: "parva"</note> quantity. — And throwing itself down, it began to descend, rolling from the high slopes <note>original: "spiagge," which in this context refers to the broad, sloping sides of the mountain</note> over the other snow. The more it sought a lower place, the more its bulk increased, so that, having finished its course, it stood upon...

<summary>In this fable, a small patch of snow on a mountain peak decides to descend to avoid the sun's heat and the sin of pride. As it rolls down, it inadvertently grows into a massive size, illustrating how humility can lead to greatness.</summary>

I wish to hide myself in some secret place, and there, in tranquil rest, pass my life. — And so, having remained hidden for several months, returning one day to the open air and coming out...

## XI. — THE FIG TREE.

The fig tree, as it stood without fruit, no one looked at it; wishing to be praised by men by producing such fruit, it was bent and broken by those very people <note>As with the walnut tree on the previous page, the fig tree’s "success" in bearing fruit leads to its physical harm by those who wish to harvest it.</note>.

## XII. — THE PLANT AND THE STAKE.

The plant complains about the old, dry stake that has been placed by its side, and of the dry stakes that surround it: [yet] one keeps it upright, and the other guards it from bad company <note>original: "triste compagnia," literally "sad company," referring here to harmful weeds or encroaching growth that the fence keeps at bay</note>.

## XIII. — THE CEDAR AND THE OTHER PLANTS.

The cedar, grown proud of its beauty, feels wary of the plants surrounding it, and having had them cleared away from its presence, the wind—no longer being broken <note>The other trees acted as a windbreak for the cedar.</note>—then threw it to the ground, uprooted <term>uprooted: "diradicato," meaning pulled out by the roots; a metaphor for total ruin caused by isolation and pride</term>.

## XIV. — THE CLEMATIS.

The clematis <term>clematis: "vitalba," or Old Man’s Beard, a vigorous climbing plant common in the Italian countryside</term>, not being content to stay within its own hedge, began to stretch its branches across the public road and attach itself to the opposite hedge; wherefore it was later broken by the travelers.

### XV. — BAD COMPANY

->DRAGS THE GOOD DOWN INTO ITS OWN RUIN.<-

The vine, having grown old upon an old tree, falls along with the ruin of that very tree; and so, because of its wretched company, it came to perish together with it <note>Leonardo often used the vine and tree as a metaphor for dependency; here, he warns that choosing a failing partner leads to one's own destruction</note>.

### XVI. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

The willow, which, by its long shoots, wishes to grow so as to surpass every other plant, was itself also always stunted <note>original: "storpiato," meaning crippled or mutilated</note> because it kept company with the vine, which is pruned every year <note>Willows were often used as living stakes to support grapevines; the willow’s growth was frequently cut back to keep it manageable for the vineyard</note>.

### XVII. — THE CEDAR.

### XXVII. — THE EAGLE.

The eagle, wanting to mock the owl, ended up with its wings stuck in birdlime <note>A sticky substance, often made from holly bark, used by hunters to trap birds</note>, and was captured and killed by a man.

### XXVIII. — THE SPIDER.

The spider, wanting to catch the fly with its deceptive webs, was cruelly killed upon them by a hornet.

### XXIX. — THE CRAB.

The crab, staying under a rock to catch the fish that entered beneath it, was surprised by a flood with a ruinous tumble of stones; and by their rolling, the crab was crushed.

### XXX. — THE DONKEY AND THE ICE.

The donkey, having fallen asleep upon the ice <note>original: *diaccio*, an archaic Tuscan form of *ghiaccio* (ice)</note> of a deep lake, his own body heat dissolved the ice; the donkey woke up underwater, to his great misfortune, and immediately drowned.

### XXXI. — THE ANT AND THE GRAIN.

The ant, having found a grain of millet <note>Though the title says wheat (*grano*), the text specifies millet (*miglio*), a common cereal in the Renaissance</note>, the grain, feeling itself seized by the ant, cried out: “If you do me the great favor of letting me fulfill my desire to be born, I will return to you a hundred of myself.” And so it was done.

### XXXII. — THE OYSTER, THE RAT, AND THE CAT.

The oyster, being unloaded near the sea at the fisherman’s house along with other fish, begged the rat to lead it to the water’s edge. The rat, having formed a plan to eat the oyster, caused it to open; but as the rat bit into it, the oyster snapped shut upon its head and held it fast. Then the cat arrived and killed the rat.

The thrushes rejoiced greatly, seeing that

for through them, they later lose all 
protection and remain bound under the power 
of their enemy, losing their liberty and 
often their lives.

### XXXVI. — THE MONKEY AND THE LITTLE BIRD.

A monkey, finding a nest of little birds, joyfully approached them; as they were already almost ready to fly, she was only able to catch the smallest one. Filled with joy, she went back to her dwelling <note>original: *ricetto*, meaning a retreat, shelter, or home</note> with it in her hand; and, beginning to contemplate this little bird, she started to kiss it. Out of her unrestrained love <note>original: *isviscerato amore*, meaning an intense, obsessive, or overwhelming affection</note>, she kissed, turned, and squeezed it so much that she took its life. This is told for those who, by failing to discipline their children, come to a bad end.

### XXXVII. — THE DOG AND THE FLEA.

Having entered into the thick wool, it began with great effort to try and pass through to the roots of the hairs; this undertaking, after much sweat, it found to be in vain, because those hairs were so thick that they almost touched one another, and there was no space where the flea could taste the skin. ### XXXVIII. — THE MOUSE, THE WEASEL, AND THE CAT.

While the mouse was besieged in its small dwelling by the weasel, who with constant vigilance waited for its destruction <note>original: *disfazione*</note>,* and through a small vent <note>original: *spiraculo*, an archaic term for a small opening or air-hole</note>, it [the mouse] gazed upon its great peril <note>original: *periculo*</note>. — Meanwhile the cat came, and suddenly seized the weasel, and immediately devoured it. ### XL. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

A spider, having found a bunch of grapes which, because of its sweetness, was frequently visited by bees and various kinds of flies, believed it had found a place very well-suited for its deception. Having lowered itself down by its thin thread and entered its new dwelling, it stayed there every day, hiding in the vents <note>original: *spiraculi*, referring to the small air-holes or gaps between the grapes</note> formed by the spaces between the individual grapes. Like a thief, it would assault the poor animals that were not on their guard against it. But after several days had passed, the grape-gatherer <term>Vendemmiatore: the laborer who performs the seasonal harvest of grapes for winemaking</term> picked those grapes and placed them with the others, and the spider was crushed along with them. Thus, the grapes became a snare and a deception for the deceiving spider, just as they had been for the deceived flies.

### XLIII. — THE LEGEND OF WINE 
### AND MUHAMMAD.²

Wine, that divine liquor of the grape, finding itself in a golden and rich cup upon the table of Muhammad <note>The text uses the archaic spelling "Maumetto"</note>, and being swollen with the glory of such great honor, was suddenly seized by a contrary thought, saying to itself: — “What am I doing? Do I not perceive that I am near my death, and about to leave the golden dwelling of this cup to enter the foul and fetid caverns of the human body, and there be transformed from a fragrant and sweet liquor into ugly and wretched urine? And as if such an evil were not enough, must I also lie for so long in those foul receptacles alongside the other fetid and corrupt matter that comes from human intestines?” — It cried out toward heaven, demanding vengeance for such an insult, and asking that an end finally be put to such contempt; and that, since that country produced the most beautiful and best grapes in all the rest of the world, they should at least not be turned into wine. ### I. — LOVE OF VIRTUE. 3

The Calandrino * <note>original: "Calendrino"; referring to the legendary bird Charadrius, often depicted in medieval bestiaries</note> is a bird of which it is said, 
that when it is brought before a sick 
person, if the said patient is to die, 
this bird turns its side to them, stays on the 
contrary side and never looks at them; 
and, if that patient is to escape death, 
this bird never lets them out 
of its sight, but rather is the cause of removing 
every illness from them.
    Similarly, the love of virtue never looks 
upon anything base or wicked, but rather always dwells 
in honest and virtuous things, and always returns home 
to a noble heart <term>cor gentile: a concept central to the "Dolce Stil Novo" school of poetry, implying that true nobility is a quality of the spirit and character rather than of birth</term>, in the likeness of birds 
in green woods upon flowering branches; 
it demonstrates this love more in adversity than 
in prosperity, acting like a light, which

## II. — ENVY.⁴

Of the kite bird <term>nibbio: the red kite, a bird of prey often used in medieval lore to represent greed or cruelty</term> it is read that, when it sees its young in the nest becoming too fat, it pecks at their ribs out of envy and keeps them without food.

## III. — JOY.⁵

Joy is attributed to the rooster, which rejoices at every little thing and sings with various and playful movements.

## IV. — SADNESS.⁶

Sadness is likened to the raven, which, when it sees its newborn chicks are white <note>In medieval bestiaries, it was a common belief that ravens were born white and were not recognized or fed by their parents until their black feathers appeared</note>, departs in great grief; with a mournful lament <note>original: "rammarichío"</note>, it abandons them and does not feed them until it sees at least a few black feathers on them.

## V. — PEACE.⁷

Of the beaver it is read that, when it is pursued by hunters, knowing it is being hunted for the medicinal power of its testicles, and being unable to flee any further, it stops; to find peace with the hunters, it bites off its own testicles with its sharp teeth and leaves them for its enemies. <note>This widely shared medieval myth was used as an allegory for the "wise man" who casts off his sins or worldly possessions to save his soul from the devil.</note>

<summary>This page presents four moral allegories using animal lore—the kite's envy of its young, the rooster's joy, the raven's sorrow over its white chicks, and the beaver's self-mutilation for survival—to illustrate human emotions and the pursuit of peace.</summary>
<keywords>Envy, Joy, Sadness, Peace, Kite bird, Rooster, Raven, Beaver, Bestiary, Moral Allegory, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

## VI. — ANGER.⁸

Of the bear it is said that when it goes to the homes of the bees <gloss>bees</gloss> to steal their honey, the bees begin to sting it. Because of this, the bear leaves the honey and rushes to take revenge; and, wishing to avenge itself against all those that bite it, it avenges itself against none. In this way, its life is turned into rage, and throwing itself upon the ground, flailing <note>original: "innaspando," a verb describing a reeling or windmilling motion, like a silk winder</note> with its paws and feet, it defends itself against them in vain.

## VII. — COMPASSION OR GRATITUDE.⁹

The virtue of gratitude is said to be greatest in the birds called hoopoes <gloss>hoopoe</gloss>, which, recognizing the benefit of the life and nourishment received from their father and mother, make a nest for them when they see them grow old. They brood over them and nourish them, and with their beaks they pluck out their old and worn feathers, and with certain herbs they restore their sight, so that they return to a state of vitality. <note>This myth of the hoopoe caring for its aged parents was a popular medieval symbol of filial piety and "Epeus," the restorative power of nature.</note>

## VIII. — AVARICE.¹⁰

The toad feeds on earth, and always remains thin because it is never satisfied; so great is its fear that the earth itself might run out. <note>In the medieval mind, the toad was a common symbol for the miser, who possesses much but lives in poverty for fear of losing what they have.</note>

### IX. — INGRATITUDE.¹¹

Doves are likened to ingratitude; for when they reach an age where they no longer need to be fed, they begin to fight with the father, and this battle does not end until they drive the father out and take his mate <note>original: "mogliera," literally wife</note>, making her their own.

### X. — CRUELTY.¹²

The basilisk <note>original: "basalisco"</note> is of such great cruelty that, when it cannot kill animals with its venomous sight, it turns to the grasses and plants, and, fixing its gaze upon them, causes them to wither.

### XI. — LIBERALITY.¹³

Of the eagle it is said that it is never so hungry that it does not leave a portion of its prey to those birds that are around it; these birds, being unable to feed themselves, must necessarily be courtiers of the eagle, because in this way they find food.

The siren <note>original: "serena," referring to the mythological creature</note> sings so sweetly that she lulls the sailors to sleep; then she climbs upon the ships and kills the sleeping sailors.

The hare is always afraid; the leaves that fall from the trees in autumn keep it in constant terror and, more often than not, in flight.

### XXIV. — CONSTANCY.²⁶

The phoenix is likened to constancy; which, understanding by its nature its own renewal, is constant in enduring the burning flames that consume it, and then it is born anew.

### XXV. — INCONSTANCY.²⁷

The swift <note>original: "rondone." Swifts were often confused with swallows or martins in bestiaries; their rapid, erratic flight made them a symbol of an unstable mind.</note> is a symbol for inconstancy; it is always in motion so as not to endure even the slightest discomfort.

### XXVI. — TEMPERANCE.²⁸

The camel is the most lustful animal that exists, and would go a thousand miles after a female camel; yet, if it lived continually with its mother or sisters, it never touches them, so well does it know how to temper itself. <note>In the Renaissance, "temperance" often referred to the control of physical appetite; here, the camel is praised for respecting natural boundaries and kin, despite its high drive.</note>

### XXVII. — INTEMPERANCE.²⁹

The alicorn or unicorn <note>original: "alicorno overo unicorno."</note>, through its intemperance and inability to control itself, because of the delight it takes in young maidens, forgets its ferocity and wildness; setting aside all suspicion, it goes to the seated maiden and falls asleep in her lap; and in this way, the hunters capture it. <note>This refers to the famous medieval legend that a unicorn could only be captured by a virgin; its "intemperance" lies in its inability to resist the pleasure of her presence.</note>

### XXVIII. — HUMILITY.³⁰

The greatest demonstration of humility is seen in the lamb; which submits itself to every animal. And when lambs are given as food to imprisoned lions, they submit themselves to them as if to their own mother; so much so that, quite often, the lions have been seen refusing to kill them. <note>This imagery likely stems from medieval menageries where the "king of beasts" was thought to recognize the innocence of the lamb.</note>

### XXIX. — PRIDE.³¹

The falcon, because of its arrogance and pride, wants to dominate and overpower all the other birds of prey, and desires to be alone; and many times the falcon has been seen to assault the eagle, the queen of birds.

### XXX. — ABSTINENCE.³²

The wild donkey, when it goes to the spring to drink and finds the water clouded with mud, will never have such a great thirst that it will not abstain from drinking, waiting until that water clears itself. <note>The "wild donkey" (onager) appears frequently in bestiaries; here, its fastidiousness is reinterpreted as the virtue of self-restraint.</note>

### XXXI. — GLUTTONY.³³

The vulture * is so subject to gluttony that it would travel a thousand miles to eat from a carcass; and for this reason, it follows (armies). <note>original: "voltore." The parenthetical "armies" (li eserciti) suggests the vulture's presence on the battlefield as a symbol of its insatiable appetite for death.</note>

### XXXII. — CHASTITY.³⁴

The turtledove <note>original: "tortora."</note> never betrays its mate, and if one dies, the other observes perpetual chastity; it never perches on a green branch and never drinks clear water. <note>In medieval folklore, the turtledove was the ultimate symbol of fidelity. It was believed that a widowed turtledove would stir the water with its feet to make it muddy before drinking and avoid green leaves, as a sign of mourning for its lost partner.</note>

### XXXIII. — LUST.³⁵

The bat <note>original: "palpistrello," an archaic form of "pipistrello."</note>, because of its unrestrained lust, does not observe any universal rule * of behavior; instead, male with male, and female with female, they engage in coitus together just as they happen to find each other.

### XXXIV. — MODERATION.³⁶

The ermine, because of its moderation, eats only once a day; and it would rather allow itself to be captured by hunters than seek refuge in a muddy den—so as not to stain its nobility. <note>The ermine was a powerful symbol of purity in the Renaissance (famously depicted by Leonardo da Vinci in "The Lady with an Ermine"). Legend held that the animal valued its white coat so much that it would choose death over the "filth" of a muddy burrow.</note>

### XXXV. — EAGLE.³⁷

The eagle, when it is old, flies so high that it burns its feathers, and nature allows it to be renewed in youth by falling into shallow water. And if its young cannot *** <note>This reflects the ancient belief in the eagle's rejuvenation (the "Aquila" myth), where the aging bird flies into the sun's heat to sear away its old plumage and the film over its eyes, then plunges into a spring to be reborn.</note>

### XXXIX. — CHAMELEON. <note>original: "camaleon"</note> ⁴¹

This creature lives on air, and within it, it masters all birds; and, to remain safer, it flies above the clouds and finds air so thin that it cannot support any bird that might follow it.
    None reach this height except those to whom it is granted by the heavens—that is, where the chameleon flies. <note>In medieval bestiaries, the chameleon was often said to live only on air. Leonardo here uniquely describes it as a high-flying creature, perhaps confusing its "aerial" nature with the habits of a bird or using it as a symbol for the elevated mind.</note>

### XL. — ALEPO FISH. ⁴²

The Alepo does not live out of the water. <note>Possibly a reference to a species mentioned by ancient naturalists like Pliny, or a local name for a fish such as the bleak.</note>

### XLI. — OSTRICH. ⁴³

This bird converts iron into its nourishment; it hatches its eggs with its gaze. Regarding arms, <margin>Said for arms, a symbol of weapons.</margin> it is the nourishment of captains. <note>It was a common medieval belief that ostriches could digest metal. The idea of hatching eggs with the eyes symbolized intense focus or the power of the spirit. Because of its "strength" in consuming iron, it became a common heraldic symbol for military leaders.</note>

### XLII. — SWAN. ⁴⁴

The swan is pure white, without any blemish, and it sings sweetly as it dies; this song brings its life to an end.

### XLIV. — CICADA.⁴⁶

This one, with its song, makes the cuckoo go silent;* <note>original: "cuculo"</note> it dies in oil and is reborn in vinegar; it sings through the burning heat. <note>The idea of an insect being "reborn" in vinegar likely stems from observations of insects appearing to revive after being preserved or cleaned in acidic solutions. In allegories, the cicada often represents the soul or the poet who thrives in the "heat" of inspiration.</note>

### XLV. — BASILISK.⁴⁷

**Cruelty.** This is fled from by all serpents. The weasel, by means of rue, fights against it and so kills it. <note>The basilisk was a legendary king of serpents whose gaze or breath could kill. Ancient tradition, popularized by Pliny the Elder, held that the scent of a weasel—or a weasel that had eaten the herb rue—was the only thing that could survive and kill the monster.</note>

### XLVI. — THE ASP, STANDS FOR VIRTUE.

This carries sudden death in its teeth; and, so as not to hear enchantments, it stops up its ears with its tail. <note>Based on a common interpretation of Psalm 58, the "deaf adder" (or asp) was said to press one ear to the ground and plug the other with its tail to avoid hearing the voice of a charmer. Leonardo uses this as a symbol of Virtue—perhaps representing a refusal to listen to flattery or corrupting influences.</note>

### XLVII. — DRAGON.⁴⁸

This entangles the legs of the elephant, and that [the elephant] falls upon it, and both of them die. And, in dying, it achieves its revenge. <note>Medieval bestiaries frequently depicted a mortal combat between the dragon and the elephant. The dragon was said to wrap itself around the elephant's legs to trip it; as the elephant fell, its massive weight would crush the dragon, resulting in the death of both.</note>

The text here cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

According to medieval legend, young vipers were thought to eat their way out of their mother’s womb, killing her in the process—a symbol of ingratitude or the destructive nature of sin.</note>

### XLIX. — SCORPION.⁵⁰

Fasting saliva <note>original: "sciliva," an archaic form of "saliva."</note> spat upon a scorpion kills it; this is similar to abstinence from gluttony, which takes away and kills the diseases that arise from that gluttony, and opens the path to the virtues.

### L. — CROCODILE, HYPOCRISY.⁵¹

This animal catches a man and kills him instantly. After he has killed him, with a mournful voice and many tears, he laments him; and, the lament being finished, he cruelly devours him. So does the hypocrite, who, for every slight thing, fills his face with tears, showing the heart of a tiger, and rejoices in his heart at the misfortune of others while wearing a piteous face. <note>This is the origin of the phrase "crocodile tears," referring to a false display of grief.</note>

### LI. — <term>TOAD</term>.* ⁵²

The toad flees the light of the sun, and if it is held there by force, it swells up <note>original: "sgonfia," used here in the archaic sense of puffing up or inflating.</note> so much that it hides its head below, and deprives itself of those rays. Thus acts the enemy of bright and shining virtue, who cannot, except with a swollen <note>original: "insgonfiato," meaning prideful or puffed up.</note> spirit, remain by force in its presence.

---
* toad. <note>The original Italian uses "Botta," an archaic/dialect term, and provides the more common "rospo" as a clarification.</note>

### LII. — THE CATERPILLAR, REPRESENTING VIRTUE IN GENERAL. 53

The caterpillar <note>The original text includes a footnote: "Understood: it symbolizes virtue."</note>, which, through the practiced study of weaving its new home around itself with marvelous artifice and delicate work, later emerges from it with painted and beautiful wings, launching itself with them toward the heavens.

### LIII. — THE SPIDER. 54

The spider gives birth from within itself to its ingenious and masterfully crafted web, which, in return, provides it with the captured prey.

### LIV. — THE LION. 55

This animal, with its thundering roar, awakens its cubs three days after they are born, opening all their dormant senses; and all the beasts that are in the forest flee. <note>In medieval bestiaries, it was a common belief that lion cubs were born dead and were brought to life on the third day by the breath or roar of their father—often used as a symbol for the Resurrection.</note>

This can be compared to the children of virtue who, through the cry of praise, are awakened and grow in honorable studies that raise them ever higher; and all the wicked <note>original: "tristi," here meaning those who are wretched or morally base.</note> flee at that cry, distancing themselves <note>original: "cessandosi," meaning moving away or departing.</note> from the virtuous.

Furthermore, the lion covers its tracks <note>original: "pedate."</note> so that its path may not be understood by its enemies. This is well-suited to captains <note>In the sense of military commanders or leaders.</note> to hide...

### LV. — THE TARANTULA. <note>original: "Taranta," a regional variant of "tarantola."</note> 56

### LVII. — THE ELEPHANT. 58

And when they are sick, lying on their backs, they cast herbs toward the heavens, as if they wished to offer a sacrifice.

### LIX. — THE SERPENT. 60

The serpent, a most massive animal, when it sees any bird in the air, draws its breath in so strongly that it pulls the birds into its mouth. Marcus Regulus, consul of the Roman army, was with his army attacked and almost defeated <note>original: "rotto," literally "broken," referring to the routing of his forces</note> by such an animal. This animal, having been killed by a siege engine <term>macchina murale: a "wall-machine" such as a catapult or ballista used for breaching fortifications</term>, was measured at 125 feet, that is 64 and a half cubits <term>braccia: a traditional Italian unit of length based on the arm</term>; with its head, it towered over all the trees of a forest.

### LX. — THE BOA. 61

This is a great snake which, with its own body, clings to the legs of a cow so that it cannot move, then it suckles from it in such a way that it almost dries the cow up. Of this species, in the time of Emperor Claudius, one was killed on the Vatican Hill which had a whole child in its body, whom it had swallowed.

## LXII. — THE BONNACON * HARMS THROUGH FLIGHT. 63

This creature is born in Paeonia <note>An ancient region in the Balkans, north of Macedonia</note>; it has a neck with a mane similar to a horse, but in all other parts it resembles a bull, except that its horns are curved inward in such a way that it cannot butt with them. Because of this, it has no other means of escape but flight, during which it discharges dung for a distance of 400 cubits <term>braccia: a traditional Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches</term> along its path—which burns like fire wherever it touches.

## LXIII. — THE BAT. 64

The more light there is, the more this creature becomes blind, and the more it looks at the sun, the more sightless it becomes. This represents Vice, which cannot remain where Virtue is present.

### LXIV. — THE PARTRIDGE. 65

This bird transforms from female to male and forgets its original sex; out of envy, it steals <note>original: "fura" — to steal or snatch away</note> the eggs of others, but those born from them follow their true mother.

### LXV. — THE SWALLOW. 66

This bird, with the swallow-stone <note>original: "celidonia" — a legendary stone said to be found in the stomachs of swallows, used here as a medicinal or magical cure for blindness</note>, gives sight to its blind-born young.

### LXVI. — THE ERMINE. 67

Moderation restrains all vices. The <term>ermine</term> <note>A stoat in its white winter coat, a symbol of purity in Renaissance heraldry</note> would rather die than soil itself <note>Legend held that the ermine would allow itself to be captured by hunters rather than retreat into a muddy burrow and stain its white fur</note>.

### LXVII. — LIONS, LEOPARDS, PANTHERS, TIGERS.

These keep their claws in their sheaths and never unsheathe them unless they are upon their prey or an enemy.

### LXVIII. — THE LIONESS. 68

When the lioness defends her cubs from the hands of hunters, so as not to be terrified by the spears, she lowers her eyes to the ground, so that her cubs are not taken captive because of her flight <note>By refusing to look at the weapons, she prevents fear from triggering her instinct to flee, thus staying to protect her young</note>.

### LXIX. — THE LION. <sup>69</sup>

This so-terrible animal fears nothing more than the noise of empty carts and, similarly, the crowing of roosters; it is greatly afraid upon seeing them and looks at their crest with a fearful expression—and it becomes greatly disheartened <note>original: "invilisce" — to lose heart, become cowardly, or lose its spirit</note> when its face is covered.

### LXXII. — THE TIGER. <sup>72</sup>

This is born in <term>Hyrcania</term> <note>An ancient region located southeast of the Caspian Sea, famously associated with tigers in Roman and Renaissance literature</note>, which is somewhat similar to the panther due to the various spots on its skin, and it is an animal of terrifying speed. Then, by the scent of the cubs, it pursues the hunter. When the hunter sees the tiger approaching, he drops one of the cubs; she picks it up and carries it to the nest, and immediately catches up to the hunter again, doing the same until he boards a boat.

## LXXIV. — THE BASILISK. ⁷⁴

This is born in the province of <term>Cyrenaica</term> <note>original: "Arenaica." It is like a snake, but it does not move by wriggling; instead, it moves upright from its middle forward. It is said that when one of these was killed with a spear by a man on horseback, its venom, traveling up the spear, killed not only the man but the horse as well. It ruins the crops, and not only those it touches, but even those upon which it breathes; it withers the grass and shatters stones. <note>The basilisk, or "little king," was a staple of medieval bestiaries, representing the deadly power of envy or sin.</note>

## LXXV. — THE WEASEL OR BELLOLA. ⁷⁵

This creature, finding the den of the basilisk, kills it with the scent of its scattered urine; the scent of this urine, however, often kills the weasel itself. <note>Leonardo uses "Donnola" and "Bellola," both Italian terms for the weasel. In natural history tradition, the weasel was the only animal capable of slaying the basilisk, though often at the cost of its own life.</note>

### LXXVI. — THE CERASTES.* ⁷⁶

These have four small movable horns; thus, when they wish to feed, they hide their whole body under the leaves except for these little horns. By moving them, it appears to birds that they are small, playful worms; because of this, the birds immediately swoop down to peck at them, and the serpent suddenly coils around them and devours them. <note>The Cerastes is the horned viper. Leonardo describes a behavior often attributed to these snakes in medieval bestiaries, though in reality, they use their horns for camouflage or to help them burrow into the sand.</note>

### LXXVII. — THE AMPHISBAENA.⁷⁷

This one has two heads, one in its usual place and the other at its tail, as if it were not enough to eject venom from a single place. <note>The Amphisbaena—from the Greek for "going both ways"—was a mythical serpent said to be able to move forward or backward with equal ease.</note>

### LXXVIII. — THE JACULUS.** ⁷⁸

This stays upon plants and launches itself like a dart; it passes through wild beasts and kills them. <note>The Jaculus, or "javelin snake," was famously described by Lucan and Pliny as a flying serpent that dropped from trees like a projectile.</note>

animal is found without a tongue, except for this one, and it alone bites by moving its upper jaw; <note>This reflects an ancient belief recorded by Aristotle and Pliny; in reality, crocodiles move their lower jaw like other animals, but their head structure makes it appear otherwise.</note> it grows up to 40 feet, it is clawed, and armored with a **leathery hide** <note>The original term "corame" refers to skin as tough as processed leather.</note> capable of withstanding any blow; by day it stays on land, and at night in the water. Seeing this, the **ichneumon*** immediately leaps into its mouth and, having pierced its stomach and intestines, finally kills it.

## LXXXII. — THE DOLPHIN.<sup>82</sup>

Nature has given such awareness to animals that, besides knowing what is advantageous to themselves, they also know the vulnerabilities of their enemies. Thus the dolphin understands how effective the sharp edges of the fins set upon its back are, and how tender the belly of the crocodile is; therefore, in their combat, the dolphin dives beneath it, slits its belly, and thus kills it. <note>This description of the dolphin’s "saw-like" fins being used as a tactical weapon against crocodiles is another lore-based observation common in Renaissance bestiaries.</note>

### LXXXIII. — THE HIPPOPOTAMUS.* 83

This animal, when it feels weighed down <note>In the medical context of the time, this refers to an "excess of blood" or humors that made the animal feel sluggish.</note>, goes searching for thorns or, wherever they may be, the remains of cut reeds; there it rubs a vein so much that it cuts it and, once the necessary amount of blood has been let out, it covers itself in mud and heals the wound. It is shaped almost like a horse, with a cloven hoof, a twisted tail, and boar-like teeth; it has a maned neck, and its skin cannot be pierced unless it is wet; it feeds on crops. It enters fields walking backward, so that it appears to have left them. <note>Leonardo repeats the ancient lore that the hippopotamus "invented" bloodletting and uses deception to protect its food source.</note>

### LXXXIV. — THE IBIS. 84

This bird bears a resemblance to the stork, and when it feels sick, it fills its crop with water and gives itself an enema** with its beak. <note>The original term "cristero" refers to a clyster or enema; ancient naturalists like Pliny the Elder claimed the ibis taught humans this medical procedure.</note>

### LXXXV. — STAGS. 85

These animals, when they feel bitten by the spider called a *phalangium*, eat crabs and thus free themselves from such poison. <note>The "falange" (phalangium) was a term used in antiquity for various venomous spiders or arachnids thought to be particularly dangerous to livestock.</note>

### XCII. — THE CHAMELEON. <gloss>92</gloss>

This creature always takes the color of the object where it perches; for this reason, they are often devoured by elephants along with the leaves upon which they rest. <note>Leonardo reflects the ancient belief that the chameleon's camouflage is so effective it becomes a danger to itself when its surroundings are eaten by large herbivores.</note>

When this bird has killed a chameleon, it purifies itself with laurel. <note>In traditional lore, the laurel was considered a plant of purification and an antidote to the perceived toxicity of the chameleon.</note>

### XCIV. — MAGNANIMITY.

The falcon catches none but large birds, and would rather die than eat meat that does not smell good. <note>This entry uses the falcon as a symbol of high-mindedness or "magnanimity," showing a preference for noble challenges and a refusal to settle for what is base or corrupted.</note>

### XCV. — THE CRANE.

Cranes, so that their king does not perish due to poor guarding, stand around him at night with stones in their feet. <note>According to natural histories like those of Pliny, cranes held a stone in one foot while standing on the other; if they fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake them.</note>
Love, fear, and reverence: write these on three crane-stones.

## XCVII. — ON FORESIGHT.

The rooster does not crow unless he first beats his wings three times; the parrot, in moving between branches, does not place its feet where it has not first <unclear>p</unclear>laced its beak. <note>Leonardo draws on the idea that the parrot uses its beak as a "third foot" for safety, symbolizing a cautious person who tests the ground before committing to a step.</note>

## XCVIII. — FOR DOING GOOD.

By the branch of the walnut tree—which is only struck and beaten when it has brought its fruit to perfection—are signified those who, upon the completion of their famous works, are struck by envy in various ways. <note>It was a common rural practice to beat walnut trees with poles to knock down the ripe nuts; Leonardo transforms this into a metaphor for how success invites criticism and jealousy.</note>

## XCIX. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

By the thorn, grafted* onto good fruit, is meant one who by nature was not disposed toward virtue, but through the help of a teacher <term>precettore</term> <note>A private tutor or mentor responsible for moral and intellectual guidance.</note> yields most useful virtues.

---

* <gloss>grafted onto it</gloss>

## C. — ON FLAX.

Flax is dedicated to the death and corruption of mortals: to death by way of the snares <note>Original: *lacciuoli*, referring to nets or nooses made of linen cord.</note> for birds, animals, and fish; to corruption because of the linen cloths in which the dead are wrapped for burial, who then decay within such fabrics. <note>Leonardo highlights the irony that the same plant used to create fine clothing and essential tools is also the primary material for the hunter's trap and the shroud of the corpse.</note>

<summary>In these four allegories, Leonardo explores the necessity of caution (foresight), the inevitability of envy following success, the transformative power of education, and the somber connection between the flax plant and human mortality.</summary>

<keywords>foresight, envy, education, mortality, rooster, parrot, walnut tree, grafting, flax, linen, snares, burial</keywords>

## THOUGHTS ON SCIENCE.

---

### I. — THEORY AND PRACTICE.

You must describe the theory and then the practice. <note>Leonardo emphasizes that intellectual understanding must precede manual execution.</note>

### II. — ON THE ERROR OF THOSE WHO USE PRACTICE WITHOUT SCIENCE.

Those who fall in love with practice without science <note>In this context, 'science' refers to *scientia*, or systematic knowledge based on principles like geometry and anatomy.</note> are like the helmsman who boards a ship without a rudder or a compass, and who never has certainty of where he is going.

Practice must always be built upon sound theory; of which *Perspective* is the guide and the gateway, and without this, nothing is done well in matters of painting.

### III. — COMPARISON OF THE PRACTITIONER.

The painter who portrays by practice and the judgment of the eye, without reason, is like the mirr- <note>The truncated word "spec-" in the original is a <term>catchword</term>, a syllable placed at the bottom of a page to help the printer or binder identify the first word of the following page (in this case, *specchio* or 'mirror').</note>

<summary>In these aphorisms, Leonardo da Vinci argues that manual artistic practice is directionless without "science"—specifically the mathematical rules of perspective—comparing a thoughtless painter to a ship without a rudder.</summary>

Science is the captain, and practice is the soldiery. <note>Leonardo uses this military metaphor to illustrate that while the "soldiers" (manual skills) do the work, they are aimless and ineffective without the "captain" (intellectual principles).</note>

### VI. — ADVICE TO THE PAINTER.

And you, painter, who desire extensive practice, must understand that if you do not build it upon a sound foundation of natural things, you will produce many works with little honor and even less profit; but if you build it well, your works will be numerous and excellent, to your great honor and much utility.

### VII. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

Here the adversary <note>The "adversary" is a rhetorical device Leonardo uses to represent the common viewpoint of uneducated craftsmen of his time.</note> says that he does not want so much science, for the practice of portraying natural things is enough for him. ### IX. — THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEORY AND PRACTICE.

->Where the science of weights is deceived by<-
->practice.<-

The science of weights <term>Statics: the study of forces and balances</term> is deceived by its practice, and, in many parts, it <insert>practice</insert> does not agree with that science, nor is it possible to reconcile them; and this arises from the pivots <note>literally "poles"</note> of the scales, by means of which the science of such weights is conducted. the arms <note>original: 'lancie'. In this context, it refers to the beams or arms of a balance scale.</note>, together with the weights <note>Note: 'that' is implied here in the original Italian.</note> placed upon them, are judged.

### X. — THE STERILITY OF SCIENCES WITHOUT PRACTICAL APPLICATION.

All sciences that end only in words have as quick a death as they have life, except for their manual part—that is, the act of writing, which is a mechanical part. <note>Leonardo argues that theoretical knowledge is fleeting unless it results in a tangible, physical application or is at least recorded through the 'mechanical' craft of writing.</note>

### XI. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

Avoid that study of which the resulting work dies along with its creator. <note>A reflection on the importance of leaving behind a legacy of useful machines, art, or documented discoveries that outlive the individual.</note>

### XII. — LEONARDO'S REMINDERS.

When you assemble the *Science of the motions of water*, remember to include, beneath each proposition, its practical applications <note>original: 'giovamenti', meaning benefits or uses</note>, so that such science may not be useless.

### XIII. — THE DISTRIBUTION OF HIS TREATISES.

When deepening a canal: do this in the book *Of the Benefits* <note>original: 'De' giovamenti'. Leonardo refers to a planned section of his work dedicated to the practical utility and advantages of his scientific discoveries.</note>, and, in proving them, cite the proven propositions; and this is the true order, because, if you wanted to show the benefit of every proposition, you would also need to create new instruments to prove such utility, and thus you would confuse the order of the forty books <note>Leonardo often mentioned his intention to organize his vast collection of observations into forty books, a goal he never fully realized in a finished publication.</note>, and likewise the order of the illustrations; that is, you would have to mix practice with theory <term>practice (pratica) and theory (teorica): In Leonardo’s time, 'practice' referred to the manual execution of a task, while 'theory' referred to the underlying mathematical and philosophical principles.</term>, which would be a confused and interrupted thing.

### XIV. — THE INTRINSIC VALUE OF KNOWLEDGE.

The acquisition of any knowledge is always useful to the intellect, because it will be able to cast off useless things and reserve the good ones. For no thing can be loved nor hated unless one first has knowledge of it. <note>This is one of Leonardo's most famous philosophical maxims, asserting that emotion must be preceded by understanding.</note>

### XV. — MAN'S NATURAL INSTINCT FOR KNOWLEDGE.

By nature, good men <note>original: 'omini boni'. In the Renaissance context, this refers to virtuous or noble-minded individuals.</note> desire to know.

<summary>Leonardo explains his organizational method for separating scientific theory from practical application to maintain clarity in his books, and offers a philosophical defense of the pursuit of knowledge.</summary>

### XVI. — PLEASURE ARISING FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF NATURE.

To the ambitious, who are not satisfied with the gift of life nor the beauty of the world, it is given as a penance that they themselves squander that very life, and that they possess neither the utility nor the beauty of the world. <note>Leonardo suggests that those obsessed with power or status are blind to the natural wonders around them, effectively punishing themselves through their own greed.</note>

### XVII. — LEONARDO AGAINST THOSE WHO DESPISE HIS WORKS.⁹⁵

I know that many will say this work is useless; these will be the ones of whom Demetrius <note>original: "Deo-metro". This likely refers to Demetrius of Phalerum or another classical philosopher; Leonardo often used idiosyncratic spellings for historical names.</note> said he made no more account of the wind which produced the words in their mouths than of the wind which came out of their lower parts. ### XVIII. — AGAINST THE DESPISERS OF SCIENCE.

Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Phalerum, a Greek philosopher. Leonardo often cited classical authorities to validate his disdain for the unlearned.</note> used to say that there was no difference between the words and voices of the unlearned ignorant and the sounds or noises caused by a belly full of superfluous wind. And he said this not without reason, for he believed there was no difference regarding from which part these people sent forth their voice—whether from the lower part or from the mouth—for both were of equal value and substance.

### XIX. — REFLECTION ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY.

It does not seem to me that coarse men of base habits and little reasoning deserve such a beautiful instrument, nor such a variety of mechanisms <note>original: "macchinamenti." Leonardo, as an anatomist and engineer, viewed the human body as a supreme biological machine.</note>, as much as speculative men and those of great discourse. To me, they deserve only a sack where food is received and from where it exits; for indeed, they should be judged as nothing more than a passage for food, because it seems to me they share nothing of the human species except for their voice and figure; and in all the rest, they are far less than a beast.

### XXIX. — TO JUDGE ONE’S OWN WORK 
### ONE MUST LOOK AT IT AFTER A LONG 
### INTERVAL.

The imitation of ancient things is more praiseworthy than that of modern things. <note>In the Renaissance context, "ancient" refers to the classical works of Greece and Rome, which Leonardo believed held a closer relationship to the fundamental truths of nature than the "modern" (medieval or early Renaissance) scholars of his era.</note>

### XLVI. — EXPERIENCE DOES NOT ERR; ONLY OUR JUDGMENTS ERR BY PROMISING THEMSELVES THINGS FROM HER THAT ARE NOT WITHIN HER POWER.

Men wrongly complain about experience, accusing her with great reproaches of being fallacious. Men wrongly complain of innocent experience, often accusing her of fallacies and false demonstrations. <note>Leonardo personifies Experience as a reliable witness, arguing that "errors" in science usually stem from human bias or poor reasoning rather than from nature itself.</note>

### XLVII. — THE NECESSITY OF THE SUCCESSION OF EFFECT TO CAUSE.

Experience never fails; it is only your judgments that fail by promising themselves effects from experience that are not produced by our experiments. Because, once a principle is given, it is necessary that whatever follows from it is a true consequence of that principle, unless it is impeded. And if an impediment does occur, the effect that should have followed from the aforementioned principle is influenced by that impediment in proportion to whether the impediment is more or less powerful than the aforementioned principle. <note>Leonardo is describing the law of causality. He argues that nature is consistent; if an experiment doesn't go as expected, it is not because nature is "failing," but because we have failed to account for a "hindrance" or competing force.</note>

### XLVIII. — THE CERTAINTY OF MATHEMATICS.

Whoever criticizes the supreme certainty of mathematics feeds on confusion, and will never be able to silence the contradictions of the <term>sophistical sciences: (scienze sofistiche) A reference to the abstract, purely verbal arguments of the university scholars of his day, which Leonardo felt led to endless debate rather than truth.</term> through which one learns nothing but an eternal clamor.

But before I proceed any further, I will perform some experiments, because it is my intention to first cite experience and then, through reason, demonstrate why such an experience is compelled to act in that manner.

## LXII. — EXAMPLE OF THE PRECEDING RULE.

*If many bodies, of equal weight and shape, are dropped one after another at equal intervals of time, the differences in their distances will be equal among them.⁹⁸* <note>original: "li eccessi de’ loro intervalli saranno infra loro eguali." Leonardo is observing the regularity of acceleration; if objects are dropped at set intervals, the space between them increases in a predictable, consistent manner.</note>

The experiment for the aforementioned conclusion on motion must be performed in this manner, namely: let two small balls of equal weight and shape be taken, and let them be dropped from a great height such that, at the start of their movement, they touch one another, and let the experimenter stand on the ground to see if their falling has kept them in contact or not. And this experiment should be repeated several times, so that no accident might hinder or invalidate such a trial—lest the experiment be false and deceive its <term>speculator: (speculatore) a person who observes and theorizes about the natural world.</term> or not.

## LXXVII. — HOW THE MASS OF WATER WHICH SURROUNDS THE EARTH HAS A SPHERICAL FORM.

This is a difficult answer; but for this reason, I would not refrain from stating my opinion. Water, "clothed" in air, naturally desires to remain united in its sphere, because in such a location it is deprived of <term>gravity</term> <note>In Leonardo's physics, an element in its "natural place" (like water in the sphere of water) loses its weight or downward pressure.</note>.
