### LXXXII. — THE ANCIENTS PROPOSED INSOLUBLE PROBLEMS.

Now observe, O reader, what we can believe of our ancestors, who sought to define what soul and life are—matters that cannot be proven—when those things which can always be clearly known and proven through experience <note>original: "isperienzia"; Leonardo uses this to mean both observation and experimental practice.</note> have remained ignored or falsely understood for so many centuries! The eye, which so clearly demonstrates its function <note>original: "offizio"; literally "office" or "duty."</note> through experience, has until my time been defined in one way by countless authors; I find through experience that it functions in quite another.

### LXXXIII. — LIMITS TO THE DEFINITION OF THE SOUL.

Although human ingenuity <note>original: "ingegno."</note> creates various inventions, using different instruments to reach the same end, it will never find an invention more beautiful, nor simpler, nor more concise than those of nature, because in her inventions nothing is lacking and nothing is superfluous. She does not utilize counterweights <note>A reference to the pulleys and weights used in the primitive robotics and machinery of Leonardo's time.</note> when she fashions limbs for movement in the bodies of animals, but instead places within them the soul of that body, which acts as its composer <note>original: "componitore"; the force that organizes and puts the body together.</note>.

### XC. — THE NECESSITY OF ANALYSIS.

We clearly know that sight is among the swiftest operations that exist, and in one instant it sees infinite forms; nevertheless, it does not comprehend more than one thing at a time. Let us take a case: you, reader, will look at this entire written page in a single glance, and you will immediately judge it to be full of various letters, but you will not know in that moment which letters they are, nor what they mean; therefore, you must go word by word, line by line, if you wish to gain knowledge of these letters. Furthermore, if you wish to ascend to the height of a building, it will be necessary for you to climb step by step; otherwise, it would be impossible to reach its height.

And so I say to you, whom Nature turns toward this art: if you wish to have true knowledge of the forms of things, you shall begin with their minute parts <note>original: "particule"—refers to the individual components or details that make up a whole.</note>, and do not move to the second [part]...

### XCI. — THE CHARACTER OF LEONARDO'S WORKS.

Begun in Florence in the house of Piero di Braccio Martelli <note>Piero di Braccio Martelli (1470–1531) was a Florentine statesman and scholar who hosted Leonardo; this specific note dates the beginning of the collection known as the Codex Arundel.</note> on the 22nd day of March 1508; and this shall be a collection without order, drawn from many papers which I have copied here, hoping later to put them in order in their proper places, according to the subjects of which they shall treat; and I believe that, before I am at the end of this, I will have to repeat the same thing many times; so, reader, do not blame me, because the matters are many and the memory cannot retain them and say: — I do not want to write this, because I wrote it before —; and if I wished to avoid falling into such an error, it would be necessary for me, for every case I wished to copy, in order not to repeat it, to always re-read everything past, especially given the long intervals of time between one writing session and the next.

### V. — THE LAWS OF NATURE ARE INESCAPABLE.

Nature does not break its law.

### VI. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

Nature is constrained by the reason <note>original: "ragione"—referring here to the governing logic or mathematical principle.</note> of its law, which lives infused within it.

### VII. — THE EFFECT FOLLOWS THE CAUSE BY NECESSITY.

When anything, being the cause of another, induces some effect through its movement, it is necessary that the movement of the effect follows the movement of the cause.

## X. — PASSIVITY AND ACTIVITY.

Many times one and the same thing is pulled by two violent forces: necessity and power. Water rains down, and the earth absorbs it by the necessity of moisture; the sun draws it up <gloss>* causes it to evaporate.</gloss> not by necessity, but by power <note>original: "potenza"—referring to an active force or capability rather than a physical requirement.</note>.

## XI. — NATURE’S PROVIDENCE
## IN THE CONFORMATION OF THE HUMAN BODY.

Because the eye is the window of the soul, the soul is always in fear of losing it, so much so that when a thing moves before it that suddenly frightens a man, he does not use his hands to protect his heart, the source of life, nor his head, the receptacle of the lord of the senses <term>Signore de' sensi: a Renaissance concept referring to the "common sense" or the part of the brain where all sensory data was thought to be gathered and judged.</term>, nor his hearing, smell, or taste; instead, the frightened sense acts instantly: not content with closing the eyes with their lids <gloss>** the eyelids.</gloss> clamped with the greatest force, it immediately turns him in the opposite direction; and not yet feeling secure, he places one hand there and extends the other, acting as a vanguard against his suspicion.

## XII. — THE PROVIDENCE OF THE DILATION AND CONTRACTION OF THE PUPIL.

*The pupil of the eye changes into as many different sizes as there are varieties of brightness and darkness in the objects presented before it.*

In this case, nature has provided a remedy for the visual faculty <term>Virtù visiva: A Renaissance term for the active power or ability of the eye to see, then believed to be a functional force within the organ.</term>, by contracting the pupil of the eye when it is harmed by excessive light, and by expanding that light <gloss>the opening through which light passes</gloss> when it is harmed by various degrees of darkness, much like the mouth of a drawstring purse. And here, nature acts like someone who has too much light in their dwelling and closes half a window, or more or less as necessary; and when night comes, they open the whole window to see better inside that dwelling. Nature employs a continuous balancing <note>original: "equazione"—here referring to a process of equalization or adjustment to maintain a constant state of clarity.</note> here, with constant tempering and adjustment, by increasing or decreasing the pupil in proportion to the darkness or brightness that is continually presented before it.

### XLIV. — ON THE PYTHAGOREAN HARMONY OF THE CELESTIAL SPHERES. <note>original: "107" — likely a reference number to a specific manuscript or note in the compiler's source.</note>

#### *Concerning the friction of the heavens, whether it produces sound or not.*

Every sound is caused by air being struck against a dense body; and if sound is produced by two heavy bodies [rubbing] against each other, it is by means of the air that surrounds them, and such friction wears away the bodies being rubbed. Therefore, it would follow that the heavens, in their friction—since they have no air between them—would generate no sound. And if such friction were indeed real, in the many centuries that these heavens have revolved, they would have been consumed by such immense speed achieved every day. Furthermore, even if they did produce sound, it could not spread, because the sound of an impact made underwater is barely heard, and it would be heard even less, or not at all, within dense bodies. Additionally: the friction of polished bodies produces no sound, which similarly happe—

<meta>catchword: happe- (Italian: acca-)</meta>

<summary>Leonardo uses mechanical logic and the laws of acoustics to debunk the ancient Greek idea of celestial harmony, arguing that because there is no air in space and the planets show no signs of physical wear, their movement must be silent.</summary>

— Why does a weight not remain in its place?
— It does not remain because it has no resistance <note>In Leonardo’s physics, "resistance" refers to a supporting medium or surface that prevents downward motion.</note>.

— And why not along other lines?
— Because a weight, having no resistance, will descend downward by the shortest path, and the lowest place is the center of the world <note>Leonardo identifies the "center of the world" as the center of the Earth, following the geocentric Aristotelian view of his era.</note>.

A glass ball, filled with cold water, sends out rays—taken from a fire—that are even hotter than the fire itself.

From these two mentioned experiments, it follows that the heat of these rays, obtained from a mirror or a ball of cold water, is hot by virtue <term>virtù</term> <note>In Leonardo’s time, "virtue" referred to the inherent power or potency of an object to act upon another—similar to how we might describe "energy" or "force" today.</note>, and not because the mirror or ball itself is hot. The same occurs in the case of the sun passing through these bodies, which heats by virtue. Because of this, some have concluded that the sun is not hot. — However, by these same cited experiments, it is proved that the sun is extremely hot; for in the experiment of the mirror and the ball, which are cold, they produce hot rays because the **primary cause** is hot. The same happens with the sun: because it is hot, when passing through such cold mirrors <note>Leonardo is likely referring to the glass of the lens or the surface of the mirror as "cold mirrors."</note>, it reflects great heat.

It is not the sun's brightness that heats, but its natural heat.

### LVI. — WHETHER THE STARS HAVE LIGHT FROM THE SUN OR FROM THEMSELVES.

Some <note>Implicitly: "the writers" or "the authors" of traditional scientific texts.</note> say that they have light from themselves, arguing that if Venus and Mercury did not have light of their own, then when they are positioned between our eye and the sun, they would darken as much of the sun as they cover from our sight. — And this is false, because it is proved that a **dark object**, placed within a **luminous one**, is surrounded and completely covered by the lateral rays of the remainder of that luminous body, and thus remains invisible. This is demonstrated when the sun is seen through the branches <term>ramificazione</term> <note>Leonardo uses the structure of bare trees to explain an optical phenomenon where a distant, thin object seems to disappear against a much larger, brighter light source.</note> of trees without leaves at a great distance; those branches do not block any part of that sun from our eyes.

The same happens with the aforementioned planets, which, even though they are without light of their own, do not occupy, as has been said, any part of the sun from our point of view.

Second proof. They say that the stars appear brightest at night the higher they are above us; and that if they did not have light from...

### LIX. — ORDER OF PROVING THAT THE EARTH IS A STAR.

First, define the eye.
Then show how the twinkling <note>original: "battere," literally "beating" or "pulsating." The footnote defines it as the trembling of light or the striking radiance of stars.</note> of any star originates in the eye; and why the twinkling of these stars is greater in one than in another; and how the rays of the stars are born from the eye. And say that, if the twinkling of the stars were, as it seems, in the stars themselves, such twinkling would appear to be a dilation as great as the body of that star. Since a star is larger than the earth, such a movement performed in an instant would be too fast to double the size of that star <note>Leonardo is using a "reduction to absurdity" argument: if stars physically expanded and contracted to cause twinkling, they would have to move faster than the laws of nature allow, therefore the effect must be optical.</note>. Then prove how the surface of the air, at the boundary of fire, and the surface of fire, at its limit <note>Leonardo refers here to the Aristotelian view of the cosmos, which held that the "sphere of fire" existed above the atmosphere as the highest of the four elemental layers.</note>, is that through which the solar rays penetrate, carrying the likeness of the celestial bodies—making them appear large in their rising and setting <note>original: "levare e porre." The footnote clarifies "porre" as "tramontare," or to set below the horizon.</note>, and small when they are in the middle of the sky.

### LXI. — THE EARTH IS NOT THE CENTER OF THE UNIVERSE.

Just as the earth is not in the center of the sun’s orbit <note>original: "cerchio del sole," literally "circle of the sun." In Leonardo's time, the movement of celestial bodies was often described in circular paths.</note>, nor in the center of the universe, it is instead in the center of its own elements, which are its companions and are united with it. To anyone standing on the moon—when she and the sun are both beneath us—this earth of ours, with its element of water, would appear to function just as the moon does for us.

### LXII. — HOW IN A DISTANT AGE THE EARTH HAD A MORE VIVID SPLENDOR.

Just as the earth, in performing the function of a moon, has lost much of its ancient light in our hemisphere due to the receding of the waters, as is proven in the fourth book: *On the World and the Waters* <note>original: "De mundo e acque." This is a reference to Leonardo's intended treatise on geology and hydrodynamics, where he argued that the Earth's brightness is primarily caused by sunlight reflecting off the oceans.</note>.

### LXIII. — QUESTIONS ON THE NATURE OF THE MOON.

1. No substance that is extremely light is opaque.
2. No lighter substance stays beneath a less light one <note>Leonardo is referring to the laws of buoyancy and the "natural places" of elements; for example, air (lighter) sits above water (heavier).</note>.
3. Whether the moon is situated in the midst of its elements or not.

## LXIV. — ON THE GRAVITY OF THE MOON.

No dense substance is lighter than air.

### LXVII. — HEAT AS THE PRINCIPLE OF LIFE.

Heat is the cause of the movement of moisture, and cold stops it, as is seen in the cold regions which halt the clouds in the air. Where there is life, there is heat; where there is vital heat, there is the movement of humors <note>original: "omore." In the science of Leonardo's time, "humors" referred to the vital fluids, like blood, that circulate through a living body.</note>.

### LXVIII. — THE EARTH IS A GREAT LIVING BEING.

Nothing is born in a place where there is no sensitive, vegetative, and rational life. Feathers grow upon birds and are changed every year; hair grows upon animals and is changed every year, except for some parts, such as the hair of the manes of lions and cats and the like; grass grows in the meadows and leaves upon the trees, and every year they are largely renewed; therefore we might say that the Earth has a vegetative soul, and that its flesh is the soil, its bones are the structures of the linkages <note>original: "collegazioni," meaning the way the rocks are joined together.</note> of the stones of which the mountains are composed, its cartilage—

<note>original: "vibrazion della terra." While "vibration" is the literal translation, Leonardo uses it here to describe the constant shifting and restructuring of the Earth's surface through geological processes.</note>

### LXXVII. — WATER IN THE RIVERS.

Among the powerful causes of earthly destruction, it seems to me that rivers, with their ruinous floods, hold the primary place. It is not fire, as some have claimed; for fire ends its devouring maw <term>voragine: literally an abyss or whirlpool, used here to describe the consuming nature of a firestorm</term> where its fuel is exhausted. The movement of water, which is maintained by the slope of the valleys, also ends and dies along with the lowest depth of the valley; but fire is caused by fuel, and the motion of water by the incline. The fuel for fire is disconnected, and so the damage will be disconnected and separate, and the fire dies where the fuel is missing. The inclination <term>declinazione: the physical slope or downward gradient of the land</term> of the valleys is continuous, and so the damage will be continuous through the ruinous course of the river, until, in the company of its valleys, it ends in the sea—the universal lowland and the only rest for the wandering waters of the rivers.

## LXXXII. — REFUTATION AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT THE SHELLS WERE CARRIED MANY DAYS' JOURNEY FROM THE SEAS BY REASON OF THE FLOOD, SO HIGH THAT IT SURPASSED SUCH AN ELEVATION.

I say that the Flood could not have carried things born in the sea to the mountains, unless the sea, in swelling, had created an inundation as far as the aforementioned places; which swelling cannot happen, because it would create a vacuum. <note>Leonardo argues based on the Aristotelian principle that nature abhors a vacuum; the sea cannot "pile up" in one place without leaving an impossible void elsewhere.</note>

And if you were to say: "the air would fill the space there"; we have already concluded that the heavy cannot be supported above the light <note>referring to the physical law that water, being heavier than air, must seek the lowest point</note>; therefore, by necessity, it is concluded that this flood was caused by rainwaters. And if this is the case, all those waters run *to* the sea, and the sea does not run *to* the mountains; and if they run to the sea, they push the shells away from the seashore and do not pull them toward themselves.

And if you were to say: — since the sea rose because of the rainwaters, it carried these shells to such a height; — we have already stated that things heavier than water do not float upon it, but stay at the bottom, from which they are not moved except by the impact of waves.

And if you were to say that the waves carried them to such high places, we have proven that in great depths, the waves at the bottom move in the opposite direction to the motion on the surface <note>Leonardo is observing the "undertow" or bottom currents that behave differently than surface waves</note>, which is made evident by the clouding of the sea from the soil taken from near the shores.

A thing lighter than water moves together with its wave and is left at the highest point of the shore by the highest wave. A thing heavier than water moves propelled by its wave along the surface and at the bottom. <note>Leonardo distinguishes between objects that float on top of a wave and heavy objects that are pushed or rolled along the seabed by the force of the water.</note> And by these two conclusions, which will be fully proven in their proper places, we conclude that the surface wave cannot carry <term>shells</term> <note>original: "nicchi"</note>, because they are heavier than water.

...rises or not, and here it will appear not to, for the reasons that will be assigned. In the Bible, we find that the aforementioned Flood consisted of 40 days and 40 nights of continuous and universal rain, and that such rain rose six cubits <note>Original: *gomiti*. A "cubit" is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm; Leonardo uses it here to reflect the biblical measurements.</note> above the highest mountain in the universe. And if this were so, and the rain were indeed universal, it would have clothed our earth in a spherical shape. A spherical surface has every one of its parts at an equal distance from the center of its sphere; therefore, the sphere of water being in this condition, it is impossible for the water upon it to move, because water does not move of its own accord unless it is descending. 

Thus, how did the water of such a great flood depart, if it is proven here to have no motion? And if it did depart, how did it move, if it did not go upwards? Here, natural reasons <note>Leonardo often contrasts "natural reasons" (the laws of physics and observation) with theological explanations.</note> fail us; therefore, to resolve such a doubt, one must call upon a miracle for help, or say that such water was evaporated by the heat of the sun.

### CIII. — ON AUTOMATIC MOVEMENTS.

Nature has arranged within man official muscles, pullers of the <term>nerves</term> <note>original: *nervi*; in Leonardo’s anatomical studies, this term often encompassed nerves, tendons, and sinews, which he viewed as a single mechanical system for pulling limbs.</note>, which are able to move the limbs according to the will and desire of the common sense, much like officials distributed by a lord throughout various provinces and cities, who in those places represent and obey the will of that lord. And that official who has most often, in a specific case, obeyed the commands given to him by word of mouth from his lord, will later perform on his own, in that same case, an action that does not deviate from the will of said lord.

Thus we often see the fingers do: having learned with the utmost obedience a piece upon a musical instrument as commanded by the judgment, after this learning, they will play it without the judgment needing to attend to it.

Do the muscles that move the legs not also perform their duty without the man even being aware of it?

### 106. — A NATURAL INSTINCT OF MAN GUIDES HIM TO SEEK HIMSELF IN THINGS AND IN BEINGS.

The painter must create his figure according to the rule of a natural body, which is generally of <term>praiseworthy proportion</term> <note>original: *proporzione laudabile*; referring to the idealized mathematical ratios of the human body common in Renaissance art theory.</note>; besides this, he should have himself measured and see in what part his own person varies much or little from that aforementioned praiseworthy standard, and, having gained this knowledge, he must take care with all his study not to fall into the same failings in the figures he creates that are found in his own person.

And from this it arises that there is no woman so ugly that she does not find some lover—unless, of course, she were monstrous.

### CVII. — ADVICE TO THE PAINTER.

The painter who has clumsy hands will make them similar in his works, and the same will happen with any limb, unless long study prevents it. ### CXII. — DECEPTION OF THE SENSES.

The eye, at the proper distances and through the proper media, is less deceived in its duty than any other sense, because it does not see except by straight lines, which compose the <term>pyramid</term> <note>original: *piramide*; in Leonardo's optical theory, the "visual pyramid" is formed by light rays traveling from the edges of an object (the base) to the point of the eye (the apex).</note> <gloss>formed by light rays</gloss> that takes the object as its base and leads it to the eye, as I intend to prove.

But the ear is greatly deceived regarding the positions and distances of its objects, because the <term>species</term> <note>original: *spezie*; in Renaissance science, "species" were the invisible forms or "images" emitted by objects that traveled through the air to reach the senses.</note> <gloss>sound waves</gloss> do not come to it by straight lines, like those of the eye, but by winding and reflected lines. Often, distant sounds seem closer than those nearby, due to the paths these species take; although the sound of an echo returns to the sense only via straight lines.

The sense of smell is even less certain of the location from which an odor originates; but taste and touch, which physically meet the object, have knowledge only of that direct contact.

### CXIII. — ON TIME.

Although time is numbered among the <term>continuous quantities</term> <note>original: *continue quantità*; Leonardo refers to things that can be divided infinitely, like a line or a flow, rather than "discrete" quantities like individual numbers.</note>, because it is invisible and without a body, it does not fall entirely under the <term>geometric power</term> <note>original: *geometrica potenza*; the mathematical domain and laws of geometry.</note>, which divides it into shapes and bodies of infinite variety, as is seen to happen with continuous visible and corporeal things. Instead, time aligns only with geometry's first principles—that is, with the **point** and the **line**. 

The point in time is to be equated to its **instant**, and the line has a resemblance to the length of a **duration of time**. And just as points are the beginning and end of the aforementioned line, so instants are the end and beginning of any given space of time. If a line is infinitely divisible, the space of a time is not immune to such division; and if the divided parts of the line are proportional to one another, then the parts of time will also be proportional among themselves. <note>Leonardo is arguing that time can be measured and understood using the same logic as a physical line on a page: just as a line consists of an infinite series of points, a duration of time consists of an infinite series of "instants."</note>

### CXIV. — ON THE CONCEPT OF TIME.

Write of the quality of time as distinct from geometry.

<vocab>time, quantity, geometric power, point, line, instant, space of time, proportional</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo explores the abstract nature of time, arguing that while it is invisible, it follows the mathematical logic of geometry, specifically comparing instants to points and durations to lines.</summary>
<keywords>philosophy of time, geometry, continuous quantity, mathematics, instants, proportionality, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### CXV. — ON THE CONCEPT OF NOTHINGNESS.

The smallest <term>natural point</term> <note>original: *punto naturale*; Leonardo refers to a physical, material speck or dot, which, however small, still occupies some physical space.</note> is greater than all <term>mathematical points</term> <note>original: *punti matematici*; in geometry, a point is a location with no width, length, or depth.</note>, and this is proven because the natural point is a **continuous quantity**, and every continuous thing is divisible to infinity, whereas the mathematical point is indivisible, because it is not a quantity.

Every continuous quantity is intellectually divisible to infinity.

Among the greatness of things that are among us, the existence of **Nothingness** <note>original: *Nulla*; Leonardo treats "Nothing" as both a philosophical void and the mathematical zero.</note> holds sovereignty, and its office extends among the things that do not have being, and its essence resides near time, between the **past** and the **future** — and it possesses nothing of the present.

This Nothingness has its part equal to the whole, and the whole to the part, and the divisible to the indivisible; it produces the same result in its division as in its multiplication, and in its addition as in its subtraction, as is demonstrated by arithmeticians by their **tenth character**, which represents this same Nothing.* And its power does not extend among the things of nature.

---

<note>* the zero.</note>

<summary>Leonardo defines "Nothingness" (the mathematical zero) as a concept that exists outside the physical world of nature, noting its unique properties in arithmetic and its relationship to the infinitesimal moment between past and future.</summary>

## VIII. — ON SPIRITS.

Up until this point, on the preceding pages, we have stated that the definition of a spirit is: — a power joined to the body, because it cannot sustain itself by its own means, nor can it take on any kind of <term>local motion</term> <note>original: *moto locale*; in Renaissance physics, this refers specifically to movement from one place to another.</note>. — And if you say that it can sustain itself; this cannot be within the elements, because if the spirit is an incorporeal quantity, such a quantity is called a vacuum, and a vacuum does not exist in nature; and even if it did exist, it would be immediately filled by the <term>collapse</term> <note>original: *ruina*; suggests the violent rush of air or water to fill an empty space.</note> of that element in which the vacuum was created.

### IX. — WHETHER THE SPIRIT POSSESSES A BODY AMONG THE ELEMENTS.

We have proven how the spirit cannot remain by itself among the elements without a body, nor can it move itself by <term>voluntary motion</term> <note>original: *moto volontario*; movement initiated by an entity's own will, as opposed to "natural motion" caused by gravity or buoyancy.</note>, unless it is directed upwards. ### XIII. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

There can be no voice where there is no movement or percussion of the air; there can be no percussion of the air where there is no instrument; and there can be no instrument that is incorporeal. This being the case, a spirit can have neither voice, nor form, nor force; and if it were to take on a body, it could not penetrate nor enter where the doors are closed. And if anyone should say: — "by means of air gathered and compressed together, the spirit takes on bodies of various forms, and through that instrument speaks and moves with force" — to this point I say, that where there are no nerves and bones, there can be no force applied in any movement made by these imagined spirits.

### XXIII. — THE FUNCTION OF PAIN IN ANIMAL LIFE.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nature has placed, in the movement of man, all those parts in front which, when struck, cause man to feel pain; and this is felt in the shins <note>original: *fusi delle gambe*; literally "the spindles of the legs."</note>, in the forehead, and the nose. This is designed for the preservation of man; for if such pain were not prepared within these limbs, the many blows received by them would certainly be the cause of their destruction.

### XXIV. — WHY PLANTS DO NOT FEEL PAIN.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If nature has ordained pain for moving souls* for the preservation of the instruments <note>original: *strumenti*; Leonardo frequently uses this mechanical term to describe biological limbs or organs.</note> which might be worn down and ruined by movement; then vegetative souls without movement** do not have to strike against the objects placed before them. Therefore, pain is not necessary in plants; thus, when they are broken, they do not feel pain as animals do.

### XXV. — THE FUNCTION OF THE PASSIONS FOR THE PRESERVATION OF LIFE.

Lust <note>original: *Lussuria*.</note> is the cause of generation.
Gluttony <note>original: *Gola*; literally "the throat," referring to the drive to eat.</note> is the maintenance of life.

Pain is the safety of the instrument <note>original: *strumento*; as noted previously, Leonardo views the body and its limbs as mechanical tools.</note>.

### XXVI. — BOLDNESS AND FEAR.

Just as boldness <note>original: *animosità*; here meaning a reckless or spirited courage.</note> is a danger to life, so fear is the security of it.

### XXVII. — THE BODY IS THE MIRROR OF THE SOUL.

He who wishes to see how the soul dwells in its body should observe how that body uses its daily habitation; that is, if the house is without order and confused, then the body held by its soul will be kept disordered and confused.

### XXVIII. — INDIPENDENCE OF THE SOUL FROM CORPOREAL MATTER.

### XXXIV. — THE BREVITY OF TIME IS AN ILLUSION OF THE MIND.

Men wrongly complain about the flight of time, blaming it for moving too fast, and failing to realize that its passage is sufficient. ### XXXV. — ILLUSIONS OF THE MIND AND THE SENSES.

Our judgment does not judge events that occurred at various intervals of time according to their proper and correct distances; for many things that passed many years ago will seem near and close to the present, while many recent things will seem ancient, linked to the distant days of our youth. <note>original: *antichità della nostra gioventù*. He who does not punish evil, commands it to be done.

He who thinks little, errs much.

Fire is associated with truth because it destroys all sophistry and lies, and the mask is associated with falsehood and lies, the hiders of what is true.

### LV. — INGRATITUDE.

Let it be left in the hands of ingratitude.
The wood nourishes the fire that consumes it. ### LVI. — ENVY.

Envy offends with concentrated infamy, that is, by detraction, a thing which terrifies virtue. 
This Envy is depicted making the "figs" <note>original: *fiche*; a vulgar gesture made by placing the thumb between the index and middle fingers, used here as a sign of contempt or defiance</note> toward heaven, because, if she could, she would use her strength against God. She is shown with a mask upon her face of beautiful appearance. She is shown as being wounded in her sight by the palm and the olive; her ear is shown wounded by the laurel and the myrtle, to signify that victory and truth offend her. <note>In Renaissance iconography, the palm and olive represent peace and victory, while laurel and myrtle represent honor and love; Leonardo suggests that the success of others is physically painful to the envious.</note> Many lightning bolts are shown coming out of her, to signify her evil speech. She is shown thin and withered, because she is in continuous torment; her heart is shown gnawed by a swelling serpent. She is given a <term>quiver</term> <note>original: *turcasso*; a case for holding arrows</note>, and the arrows are tongues, because she often offends with them. She is given a leopard's skin, because that animal kills out of envy

### LVII. — FAME.

Fame alone rises to heaven, because virtuous things are friends to God; Infamy should be depicted upside down, because all its operations are contrary to God and are directed toward the underworld. 

Fame should be painted with her whole body covered in tongues instead of feathers, and in the form of a bird. <note>This imagery is inspired by classical descriptions, such as Virgil’s *Aeneid*, where Rumor/Fame is a feathered monster with an eye and a tongue under every feather.</note>

...turned away, because they are contrary to each other; they are depicted as being founded upon the same body, because they have the same foundation: for the foundation of Pleasure is toil and Displeasure <note>original: *Dispiacere*; in this context of dualities, it refers to Pain or Sorrow</note>, while the foundation of Displeasure is various and lewd pleasures. And therefore, he is represented here with a reed in his right hand, which is hollow and without strength, and the pricks made with it are poisonous. Reeds are used in Tuscany as supports for beds <note>Leonardo uses a local Florentine custom—using Arundo donax reeds to support mattresses—as a metaphor for the "hollow" foundations of physical comfort</note>, to signify that it is there that vain dreams occur, and there a great part of life is consumed; there much useful time is thrown away—namely, that of the morning, when the mind is sober and rested, and thus the body is fit to take on new labors. Furthermore, many vain pleasures are taken there, both with the mind—imagining things impossible to oneself—and with the body, taking those pleasures which are often the cause of the failing of life; so for this reason, the reed is held for such foundations.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo's comparison between human and animal physiology, specifically focusing on the anatomical reasons for the superior senses of predators like lions, before shifting into a moral critique of human cruelty.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>
<header>MORALITY.</header>

...less ingenious and of parts less capable of receiving the power of the senses.

I have observed in the lion species that the sense of smell is formed from a part of the substance of the brain <note>original: *celabro*; an archaic term for the brain or cerebellum</note>, and it descends into the nostrils, which serve as a spacious receptacle for the sense of smell. This sense enters through a great number of cartilaginous chambers, with many passages leading toward the aforementioned brain. The eyes of the lion species occupy a large portion of their head as their receptacle, and the optic nerves connect directly to the brain. In humans, the opposite is observed: the eye sockets are but a small part of the head, and the optic nerves are thin, long, and weak; because of this weak operation, we see little by day and even worse at night, whereas the aforementioned animals see more at night than during the day. The proof of this is seen in how they hunt by night and sleep by day, as nocturnal birds also do.

### LXI. — LEONARDO’S CLASSIFICATION.

**MAN** — the description of man, in which are included those who are of a nearly similar species, such as the baboon, the monkey, and the like, which are many. <note>Leonardo’s anatomical studies led him to recognize the physical similarities between humans and primates long before modern evolutionary theory established a formal link.</note>

### LXII. — MAN AS AN ANIMAL.

On the gait of man. The walking of man is always in the manner of the universal gait of four-legged animals; for just as they move their feet in a cross <note>original: *in croce*; referring to diagonal or contralateral movement</note> like the trot of a horse, so man moves his four limbs in a cross; that is, if he thrusts forward his right foot to walk, he thrusts forward the left arm with it, and always continues in this way.

### LXIII. — THERE IS A GRADUAL TRANSITION FROM ANIMALS TO MAN.

Make a specific treatise on the description of the movements of four-legged animals, among which is man, who also in infancy goes upon four feet. <note>Leonardo often sought "universal laws" of movement that applied to all living creatures, seeing the human infant’s crawling as a link to the rest of the animal kingdom.</note>

### LXIV. — THE EVOLUTION OF FASHION.

In my day, I remember having seen in my childhood <note>original: *puerizia*</note> men both small and great...

---

### I. — PREFACE.

With rightful lamentation, <term>Painting <note>In the Renaissance, painting was often considered a "mechanical art" (manual labor). Therefore, O writers, you have wrongly excluded her from the number of these <term>liberal arts</term>, seeing that she concerns herself not only with the works of nature, but with infinite things that nature never even created.

Painting has its purpose communicable to all the generations of the universe, because its purpose is the subject of the <term>visual power <note>In the Renaissance, the "visual power" (virtù visiva) was considered an active faculty of the eye to perceive the world.</note></term>, and it does not pass through the ear to the <term>common sense <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "common sense" (senso comune) was the internal faculty that gathered and organized data from the five physical senses.</note></term> in the same way that it passes through the sight.

And it satisfies not only the human species, but other animals as well: as was shown in a painting, a likeness of a father of a family, which was caressed by his little children who were still in swaddles, and similarly by the dog and cat of the same house—it was a marvelous thing to behold such a spectacle.

### IV. — PAINTING CANNOT BE DISSEMINATED.

Those sciences which are <term>imitable <note>Leonardo uses "imitable" to mean "teachable through rote learning or copying."</note></term> are such that by them the disciple becomes equal to the author, and similarly produces his own fruit. These are useful to the imitator, but they are not of such excellence as those which cannot be left as an inheritance, like other material goods.

Among these, Painting is the first.

## VII. — REPRESENTATION AND DESCRIPTION.

Painting represents the works of nature to the senses with more truth and certainty than words or letters do; however, letters represent words with more truth than Painting does. But we shall say that the science which represents the works of nature is more admirable than that which represents the works of the maker <note>original: "opere dell' operatore." Here, Leonardo distinguishes between God's creations (Nature) and man's creations (language).</note>—that is, the works of men, which are words, such as Poetry and the like, which pass through the human tongue.

### XIII. — CONTINUATION ON PAINTING AND POETRY.

Painting is a poetry that is seen and not heard, and poetry is a painting that is heard and not seen. Therefore, these two poetries—or, if you prefer, two paintings—have exchanged the senses through which they ought to penetrate the intellect. Because, if both are painting, they must pass to the **common sense** <term>common sense: In Renaissance psychology, the "senso comune" was a faculty in the brain where all sensory inputs (sight, sound, etc.) were gathered and coordinated before being judged by the intellect.</term> through the most noble sense, which is the eye; and if both are poetry, they must pass through the less noble sense, which is hearing.

Therefore, we shall give painting to the judgment of one born deaf, and poetry shall be judged by one born blind. He does not realize that when he mentions the limbs of such beauty, time divides his words from one another; it interposes **forgetfulness** <note>original: "oblivione." # XVII. — HOW THE SCIENCE OF ASTROLOGY IS BORN FROM THE EYE, BECAUSE THROUGH IT, IT IS GENERATED.

No part exists in <term>Astrology</term> <note>original: "Astrologia." In the Renaissance, this term frequently encompassed both astronomy (the scientific study of stars) and astrology (the influence of stars on human affairs).</note> that is not the function of visual lines and <term>Perspective</term>, the daughter of <term>Painting</term>—because it is the painter who, out of the necessity of his art, gave birth to Perspective. This science cannot be achieved without lines, within which are enclosed all the various figures of bodies generated by nature; without these lines, the art of the geometer is blind.

And if the geometer reduces every surface surrounded by lines to the figure of a square, and every body to the figure of a cube, and <term>Arithmetic</term> does the same with its square and cube roots; these two sciences extend only to the knowledge of **quantity**, both continuous and discontinuous <note>Leonardo refers to the classical division of mathematics: continuous quantity (geometry) and discontinuous quantity (number/arithmetic).</note>. However, they do not concern themselves with **quality**, which constitutes the beauty of nature’s works and the ornament of the world.

### XXIII. — HOW MUSIC OUGHT TO BE CALLED THE SISTER AND THE YOUNGER OF PAINTING.

Music is to be called nothing other than the sister of Painting, given that it is the subject of hearing—the sense second to the eye—and it composes harmony through the joining together of its proportional parts, which are produced at the same moment, and are forced to be born and die in one or more harmonic intervals <note>original: "tempi armonici." In Renaissance music theory, this refers to the rhythmic durations or beats that define the structure of a composition.</note>. These intervals encompass the proportionality of the members <note>The individual notes or components of a musical phrase.</note> from which such harmony is composed, in no other way than the line [does in a drawing]—

### XXVII. — THE CAUSE OF THE LOW ESTEEM IN WHICH PAINTING IS HELD.

# THE PAINTER AND PAINTING.

---

## I. — THE VASTNESS OF THE FIELD OF PAINTING.

Everything that is visible is included within the science of painting.

## II. — THE ORIGIN OF PAINTING.

How the first painting consisted only of a single line, which traced the shadow of a man cast by the sun upon the walls.

## III. — HOW THE PAINTER IS THE LORD OF EVERY KIND OF PEOPLE AND OF ALL THINGS.

If the painter wishes to see beauties that would make him fall in love, he is the Lord who can generate them; and if he wishes to see monstrous things that terrify, or things that are buffoonish and laughable, or truly pitiable, he is their Lord and God; and if he wishes to generate landscapes and deserts, shady or gloomy places in hot weather, he [creates] them <note>The sentence ends abruptly here in the original manuscript.</note>

## X. — HOW THE PAINTER SHOULD BE EAGER TO HEAR, WHILE CREATING HIS WORK, THE JUDGMENT OF EVERY MAN.

Certainly, one should not refuse the judgment of any person while he is painting; for we know clearly that a man, even if he is not a painter, will have knowledge of the form of another man, and will judge well if he is hunchbacked, or has a shoulder that is too high or too low, or if he has a large mouth or nose or other defects <note>original: "mancamenti" — shortcomings or physical flaws.</note>. And if we know that men are able to truthfully judge the works of nature, how much more must we admit that they can judge our errors? For we know how much a man deceives himself in his own works; and if you do not recognize this in yourself, observe it in others, and you will profit from their mistakes.

Therefore, be eager to hear the opinions of others with patience; and consider carefully and think well whether the critic <note>original: "biasimatore" — one who finds fault or censures.</note> has cause or not to criticize you. And if you find that he does, correct <note>original: "racconcia" — to mend, fix, or set right.</note> the work; and if you find he does not, pretend you did not understand him or...

## XI. — ON THE POOR EXCUSE MADE BY THOSE WHO FALSELY — AND UNWORTHILY CALL THEMSELVES PAINTERS.

There is a certain breed of painters who, because of their lack of study, find it necessary to live under the beauty of gold and azure <note>This refers to the practice of using expensive pigments like gold leaf and lapis lazuli (ultramarine blue) to mask a lack of technical skill in drawing or composition.</note>. These men, with the utmost foolishness, allege that they do not produce good work because of poor payment, claiming they would know how to do as well as any other if they were only well paid. Now, see what foolish people! Such men do not know how to keep some good work on hand so they might say: "This one is for a high price; this is for a medium price; and this is of this sort <note>original: "di sorte" — meaning of a common or lower variety.</note> *"; and thus show that they have work available for every price.

And above all, the mirror must be taken as your master—that is, the <term>flat mirror</term> <note>original: "specchio piano"; Leonardo favored the flat mirror as an objective "judge" because its two-dimensional surface mimics the challenges of a painter's canvas.</note>—because upon its surface, things bear a similarity to <term>painting</term> in many respects.

That is to say, you see a painting made upon a flat surface demonstrating things that appear to be in relief, and the mirror on a flat surface does the same; the painting is a single surface, and the mirror the same; the painting is intangible, in that what appears round and prominent cannot be grasped with the hands, and the mirror does the like; the mirror and the painting show the likeness of things surrounded by <term>shadow and light</term> <note>original: "ombra e lume"; the Italian foundation of what we now call chiaroscuro, used to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume through contrast.</note>; both appear to exist far beyond their actual surface.

### XIII. — PRECEPT FOR THE PAINTER.

Every branch and every fruit is born above the base of its leaf, which serves as its <gloss>acts as its mother</gloss> mother by providing it with the water of the rains and the moisture of the dew that falls from above at night; and many times, it shields them from the excessive heat of the sun’s rays.

Therefore, you, painter, who do not possess such rules—to avoid the blame of those who are knowledgeable—be eager to depict everything from nature, and do not despise study as those do who work only for profit. <note>original: "guadagnatori"; Leonardo often criticized "money-makers" or commercial artists who prioritized speed and earnings over the deep, scientific study of natural laws.</note>

### XIV. — PAINTING IS A FIGURATIVE DISCOURSE.

Men and words are established things; and you, painter, if you do not know how to operate your figures, you are like the orator who does not know how to use his words. <note>Leonardo views painting as a form of visual rhetoric or "discorso figurato." Just as a speaker must master grammar and vocabulary to move an audience, a painter must master the "language" of anatomy and gesture.</note>

## XVI. — ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

I say that one must first learn the limbs and their workings <note>original: "travagliamenti"; this refers to the complex mechanical interactions of muscles and joints during movement.</note>, and once such knowledge is finished, one must follow the actions according to the accidents <note>original: "accidenti"; in Renaissance theory, these are the spontaneous movements or "accidental" physical reactions caused by a person's emotions or external circumstances.</note> that happen to a man; and third, to compose the histories <note>original: "storie"; narrative paintings—often biblical or classical—that were considered the highest test of an artist's skill.</note>, the study of which shall be made from natural actions, performed by chance through their circumstances. Observe these in the streets, squares, and fields, and note them with a brief description of outlines <note>original: "liniamenti"; here referring to a quick shorthand sketch.</note>: that is, for a head, make an O, and for an arm, a straight or bent line, and do the same for the legs and torso; and then, returning home, develop such reminders into perfect form.

The adversary says that to become practiced and to produce many works, it is better that the first period of study be spent in copying various compositions made on paper or walls by different masters, and that in those, one acquires quick practice and good habit. ### XVII. — ON THE WAY TO LEARN WELL HOW TO COMPOSE FIGURES TOGETHER IN NARRATIVE PAINTINGS.

When you have learned Perspective well, and have committed to memory all the limbs and bodies of things, you should frequently take delight, while going about for your pleasure, in seeing and considering the positions and actions of men while speaking, while arguing, or laughing, or fighting together; observe what actions are in them, and what actions are made by the bystanders, the peacemakers <note>original: "spartitori"; those who step in to separate people during a fight.</note>, or the onlookers of these things; and note these with brief marks, in this manner, in a small notebook of yours. This you should always carry with you, and let it be of tinted paper <note>original: "carte tinte"; paper prepared with a colored ground, typically used for drawing with a metal stylus (silverpoint), which creates a permanent mark that cannot be easily erased.</note>, so that you do not have to erase, but rather move from an old one to a new one; for these are not things to be erased, but rather preserved with great diligence. Because the infinite forms and actions of things are so many that the memory is not capable of retaining them; therefore, you shall keep these as your authors and masters.

### XVIII. — ON STUDYING EITHER WHEN YOU WAKE OR BEFORE YOU FALL ASLEEP IN BED, IN THE DARK.

I have experienced in myself that it is of no small benefit, when you find yourself in the dark in bed, to go over in the imagination <note>original: "imaginativa"; the mental faculty of forming or recalling images</note>, repeating the surface outlines of the forms previously studied, or other noteworthy things understood through subtle contemplation <note>original: "speculazione"; here meaning deep theoretical or mental investigation</note>; and this is truly a praiseworthy act, and useful for fixing things in the memory.

## COMPARISON OF PAINTING WITH SCULPTURE.

---

### I.

Having practiced Sculpture no less than Painting, and performing both to the same degree, it seems to me that I can—with little risk of bias—give a verdict on which of the two is of greater genius, difficulty, and perfection. First, Sculpture is subject to certain lights—namely, those from above—whereas painting carries its own light and shadow with it everywhere. Therefore, light and shadow are the essential elements of Sculpture. In this case, the sculptor is aided by the nature of the relief <note>original: "rilievo"; the physical three-dimensional form of the work</note>, which generates them on its own, while the painter, by acci... <note>The text cuts off here; likely intended to say "accidentalità," referring to the painter's need to artificially create the "accidents" or effects of light and shadow through skill.</note>

### II.

Sculpture is not a science, but a **most mechanical art**, because it produces sweat and physical fatigue in its practitioner; for such an artist, the simple measurements of the limbs and the nature of movements and poses are sufficient, and thus it ends in itself, showing to the eye exactly what it is. It does not inspire wonder in its observer in the way that Painting does, which on a flat surface, by the power of science, demonstrates vast landscapes with distant horizons. <note>Leonardo argues that sculpture is "literal"—it is a 3D object—whereas painting is "scientific" because it creates a world that isn't physically there.</note>

### III.

Between Painting and Sculpture I find no other difference than this: the sculptor carries out his works with greater physical exertion than the painter, and the painter carries out his works with greater mental exertion. This is proven to be true because the sculptor, in making his work, uses the force of his arms and hammering to wear away the marble or other excess stone that exceeds the figure enclosed within it <note>This reflects the Renaissance idea that the statue already exists inside the block of stone, and the artist merely "liberates" it by removing the excess.</note>...

<summary>Leonardo argues that sculpture is a "mechanical" labor focusing on physical effort and simple measurement, whereas painting is a "science" of the mind that uses perspective to create illusions of vast space.</summary>

For the painter sits with great ease before his work, well-dressed, and moves the lightest brush with lovely colors. He is adorned with garments as he pleases, and his home is full of lovely paintings and is clean; he is often accompanied by music or readers of various and beautiful works, which—without the noise of hammers or other mixed sounds—are heard with great pleasure.

### IV.

There is no comparison between the talent, artifice, and discourse <note>original: "discorso"; in this context, it refers to the intellectual reasoning or logic behind the art</note> of Painting and that of Sculpture, which does not trouble itself with **Perspective** <term>Perspective: the mathematical system used to create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface</term>, because perspective in sculpture is caused by the nature of the material and not by the skill of the artist.

...replace the material removed in excess from his work, as the painter can; to this it is answered that he who removes too much understands little, and is not a master. For if he has the measurements in his power, he will not remove what he should not; therefore we shall say that such a defect belongs to the operator and not to the material. But I do not speak of these men, for they are not masters, but **spoilers of marble**.

Masters do not trust the judgment of the eye, because it always deceives—as is proven by anyone who wishes to divide a line into two equal parts by eye alone, for experience often shows him to be wrong. Thus, because of this suspicion, good judges are always fearful—which the ignorant are not. For this reason, with the knowledge of the measurements of every length, thickness, and width of the limbs <note>original: "membri"; Leonardo refers here to the anatomical proportions of a figure</note>, they are constantly guiding themselves, and by doing so, they do not remove more than they should.

But **Painting** is of marvelous artifice <term>Artifice: the skill and ingenuity used in creating a work of art</term>, entirely composed of the most subtle speculations <note>In Leonardo's time, "speculation" referred to deep intellectual investigation and mental theory</note>, of which **Sculpture** is entirely deprived, because it involves very limited reasoning <note>original: "discorso"; referring to the intellectual logic or "discourse" behind the artistic process</note>.

One responds to the sculptor who says that his science is more permanent than Painting, that such permanence is a virtue of the sculpted material and not of the sculptor; and in this—

<summary>Leonardo argues that sculpture's permanence is a quality of the stone rather than the artist, and asserts that painting is an intellectually superior pursuit based on scientific reasoning and subtle observation.</summary>

## V.

**Painting** involves a greater mental discourse <term>Discorso mentale: the intellectual reasoning and internal logic required to translate the three-dimensional world onto a flat surface</term> and greater artifice <note>In the Renaissance, "artifice" referred to the ingenious skill and technical mastery of the artist, rather than something "artificial" or fake</note> and wonder than **Sculpture**. This is because necessity compels the painter’s mind to transform itself into the very mind of nature, acting as an interpreter between nature and art. By doing so, the painter explains the causes of nature's manifestations as governed by its own laws: how the likenesses of objects surrounding the eye converge with their true images <note>original: "simulacri"; Leonardo uses this to describe the visual forms or "species" that objects emit, which travel through the air to reach the viewer</note> at the pupil <note>original: "popilla"</note> of the eye.

Painting also determines which objects of equal size will appear larger to that eye; among equal colors, which will appear more or less dark, or more or less light; among things of equal depth, which will appear more or less deep; or among those placed at an equal height, which will appear more or less high; and why, among equal objects placed at various distances, one will appear less distinct than the other.

And such an art embraces and contains within itself all visible things, which cannot be done by...

...the poverty of **Sculpture**, namely: the colors of all things and their diminutions <note>Leonardo refers to "diminution" of color, where colors lose their intensity and change hue as they recede into the distance</note>; this [art of painting] depicts transparent things, whereas the sculptor will merely show you the natural ones <note>The sculptor relies on the actual transparency of a material like marble or glass, rather than creating the *illusion* of transparency through skill</note>, without his own artifice. The painter will show you various distances with variations of color, caused by the air interposed between the objects and the eye; he shows the mists through which the visual forms <term>Species (spezie): in Renaissance optics, these were the "images" or "likenesses" that objects were thought to shed, which then traveled through the air to the viewer's eye</term> of objects penetrate with difficulty; he shows the rains, which reveal behind them the clouds with mountains and valleys; he shows the dust, which reveals within and behind it the combatants who stir it up; he shows smoke, in varying degrees of density. 

This art will show you the fish playing between the surface of the water and the bottom; it shows the polished pebbles of various colors resting upon the washed sands of the riverbeds, surrounded by waving plants beneath the surface of the water; it shows the stars at different heights above us, and so many other innumerable effects to which **Sculpture** does not attain.

### VI. — CONCLUSION.

**Sculpture** lacks the beauty of colors, it lacks the perspective of colors, and it lacks the perspective and blurring of the boundaries <note>original: "termini"; this refers to "sfumato," Leonardo's technique of softening edges to create a sense of depth and atmosphere</note> of things remote from the eye, because...

## I. — AN EFFECT OF CLOUDS OVER LAKE MAGGIORE.

I have already seen such a multiplication of the air <gloss>a condensation of clouds in the atmosphere</gloss>, and once above Milan, looking toward Lake Maggiore, I saw a cloud in the shape of a massive mountain, full of fiery crags, because the rays of the sun—which was already at the horizon and glowing red—tinted the cloud with its own color. This cloud attracted to itself all the small clouds that were surrounding it; and the great cloud did not move from its position, but rather it retained the light of the sun at its peak until an hour and a half into the night <note>Time was often measured starting from sunset; "an hour and a half into the night" indicates the peak was so high it remained illuminated long after the ground was in darkness.</note>, so immense was its size. Within two hours of the night, it produced such great winds that it was a stupendous and unheard-of thing.

<summary>A vivid scientific observation of a massive cloud formation over Lake Maggiore that mimicked the appearance of a mountain and remained illuminated by the sun long after sunset before generating a violent storm.</summary>

## II. — AN ASCENT OF MONTE ROSA.

I say that the blue in which the air reveals itself is not its own color, but is caused by warm moisture, evaporated into tiny and imperceptible atoms, which catches the impact of the sun's rays and becomes luminous against the obscurity of the immense darkness of the region of fire <note>In the cosmological view of Leonardo's time, the "region of fire" was the uppermost sphere of the elemental world, located above the air and below the heavens.</note>, which covers it from above like a lid.

And this will be seen, as I saw it, by anyone who goes atop Momboso, <margin>Mount Rosa.</margin> a ridge of the Alps that divides France from Italy. This mountain has its base giving birth to the four rivers that flow in four opposite directions through all of Europe: and no mountain has its base at such an altitude. <note>Leonardo likely refers to the Rhine, Rhône, Po, and perhaps the Danube or Inn, though his geographical placement of their specific source at Monte Rosa reflects the era's limited cartographic precision.</note>

This mountain rises to such a height that it almost passes beyond all the clouds, and snow rarely falls there, but only hail in the summer when the clouds are at their greatest height; and this hail is preserved there in such a way that, if it were not for the rarity of clouds falling or rising there—which does not happen twice in a lifetime <note>original: "che non accade due volte in una età"</note>—there would be an immense quantity of ice <gloss>diaccio</gloss> there, built up from the layers of hail.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci describes his ascent of Monte Rosa (Momboso), using the experience to explain why the sky appears blue and to observe unique high-altitude weather patterns involving hail and ice.</summary>
<keywords>Monte Rosa, Momboso, Alps, atmospheric optics, blue sky, region of fire, glaciology, meteorology, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### V. — VARIOUS COLORATIONS OF THE SEA.

The undulating sea has no single color, but to one who sees it from the mainland, it is dark in color, and all the darker the closer it is to the horizon; and there one sees certain glimmers or reflections <gloss>lustri</gloss>, which move slowly like white sheep in a flock; and one who sees the sea while being on the high seas sees it as blue. ### VI. — THE VEGETATION OF A HILL.

Those grasses and plants will be paler in color the thinner and more lacking* in moisture <note>original: *umore*. In Renaissance science, "humors" were the vital fluids of living things; here, it refers to the sap and water content that gives plants their vibrant color.</note> the soil that nourishes them is; the soil is more lacking and thin atop the rocks that form the mountains. And the trees will be smaller and more slender the closer they get to the summits of the mountains; for the soil is thinner as it nears those mountain summits, while the soil is more abundant in richness <note>original: *grassezza*, literally "fatness," describing the fertile, nutrient-dense soil found in lowlands.</note> the closer it is to the hollows of the valleys.

Therefore, you, the painter, shall show on the mountain summits the rocks of which they are composed, largely bare of soil; and the grasses that grow there should be tiny and thin, and for the most part faded and dry due to the lack of moisture; and let the sandy and thin earth be seen showing through <gloss>transparire</gloss> between the pale grasses; and depict the tiny plants as stunted and aged at a very small size, with short and dense branchings.

### VII. — ON THE METHOD OF REPRESENTING A NIGHT SCENE.

That thing which is entirely deprived of light is total darkness. Night being in such a condition, if you wish to represent a <term>narrative scene</term> <note>original: *storia*; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to a complex figurative composition illustrating a historical, biblical, or mythological event.</note> therein, you must ensure that, there being a large fire, the object closest to said fire is most tinted by its color. This is because whatever is nearest to an object partakes most in its nature. If you make the fire tend toward a red color, you must make all things illuminated by it also appear reddish; and those that are further from the said fire should be more tinted by the black color of the night. 

The figures that are between you and the fire will appear dark against the gloom of the night rather than the brightness of the fire; those situated to the sides should be half in shadow and half reddish; and those that can be seen beyond the edges of the flames will be entirely illuminated by a reddish light against a black background.

Regarding their actions, make those who are nearby shield themselves with their hands and cloaks as a protection against the excessive heat, and with their faces turned in the opposite direction, show them flee—

<meta>catchword: flee— (original: fug-)</meta>

### VIII. — HOW TO REPRESENT A STORM.

If you wish to well represent a <term>storm</term> <note>original: *fortuna*; while this word often means "fortune," in Renaissance Italian and maritime contexts, it specifically refers to a violent tempest or gale.</note>, consider and arrange its effects carefully: when the wind, blowing over the surface of the sea and the land, removes and carries with it those things that are not firmly fixed, along with the general surge.

And to represent this storm well, first make the clouds shredded and broken, driving in the direction of the wind, accompanied by sandy dust lifted from the seashores, and branches and leaves raised by the power of the wind’s fury, scattered through the air along with many other light objects. The trees and grasses should be bent to the ground as if showing a desire to follow the course of the winds, with branches twisted out of their natural growth and the leaves tangled and turned over. The men who are found there, some should be fallen and entangled in their clothes and the dust, appearing almost unrecognizable; and those who remain standing, let them be behind some tree, embracing it to

The air should be terrifying because of the dark gloom created by the dust, mist, and thick clouds.

...thus: dust, because it is an earthy and heavy substance, even though it easily rises and mixes into the air due to its fineness, nonetheless naturally settles back down. Its highest reach is composed of its finest particles; therefore, it will be least visible and appear almost the color of the air. Smoke, which mixes within the dust-laden air, will appear as a dark cloud as it rises to a certain height, and at the highest points, smoke will be more readily seen than dust.

Smoke will tend toward a somewhat bluish color, while dust will retain its natural color. On the side from which the light comes, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear much brighter than on the opposite side. The more the combatants are immersed within this turbulence, the less visible they will be, and the less difference there will be between their highlights and their shadows.

You shall make the faces, the figures, the air, and the <term>musketeers</term> <note>original: *scoppettieri*; soldiers armed with the *scoppietto*, an early type of firearm or hand-cannon.</note> together with those near them, take on a reddish glow; and this redness will fade the further it moves from its source. Figures positioned between you and the light, if they are distant, will appear dark against a light background. Their legs, as they get closer to the ground, will be less visible because the dust is thicker and denser there.

The teeth should be parted as if in a cry of lamentation. One hand should shield the fearful eyes, turning the back of it toward the enemy; the other should rest on the ground to support the raised torso.

You shall make others crying out with their mouths wide open and fleeing; you shall make many kinds of weapons among the feet of the combatants, such as broken shields, lances, broken swords, and other similar things. You shall make dead men, some half-covered by dust, others where the dust—mixing with the spilled blood—is transformed into red mud; and the blood, in its true color, is seen flowing in a winding path from the body into the dust. Others, in the act of dying, should be clenching their teeth or rolling their eyes, clutching their fists to their bodies, with their legs twisted. One might see someone disarmed and struck down by the enemy turning toward his foe, with biting and scratching performing a cruel and...

### X. — REPRESENTATION OF THE DELUGE.

The air was dark with thick rain, which, in its oblique descent, bent by the cross-current of the winds, formed waves in the air, much like those seen in drifting dust; it varied only because such an inundation was crisscrossed by the streaks <note>original: *liniamenti*; Leonardo refers here to the visual effect of "hatching" or lines created by falling rain in a painting</note> made by the descending drops of water. But its color was dictated by fire, generated by the bolts <note>original: *saette*; lightning bolts</note> that cleave and tear through the clouds, the flashes of which struck and opened up the great expanses of water <note>original: *pelaghi*; literally "seas" or "abysses," here describing the deep floods filling the valleys</note> in the submerged valleys; these openings revealed within their churning depths <note>original: *vertici*; referring to the troughs or whirlpools in the water</note> the bent tops of trees. And Neptune <note>The Roman god of the sea, often used by Leonardo as a personification of water’s power</note> could be seen in the midst of the waters with his trident, and Aeolus <note>The ruler of the winds in classical mythology</note> was seen with his winds entangling floating, uprooted trees mixed within the immense waves.

The horizon, along with the entire hemisphere, was turbulent and fiery from the flashes of constant lightning. Men and birds were seen filling the large trees that were still exposed above the spreading waves, which formed hills surrounding the great abysses <note>original: *baratri*; deep pits or chasms</note>.

### XII. — THE ISLAND OF CYPRUS.

From the southern shores of Cilicia <note>an ancient region on the south coast of Asia Minor, in modern-day Turkey</note> one sees to the south the beautiful island of Cyprus, which was the kingdom of the goddess Venus; and many, incited by her beauty, have broken their ships and rigging among the rocks, surrounded by the swirling waves. Here the beauty of the sweet hill invites wandering sailors to refresh themselves among its flowering greenery, through which the winds, swirling around, fill the island and the surrounding sea with sweet odors.... ...ours, I entered the city of Calindra,* situated near our borders.

This city is located on the slopes of that part of Mount Taurus which is divided by the Euphrates, and it looks toward the peaks <note>original: "corni," literally horns</note> of the great Mount Taurus to the west.

These peaks are of such height that they seem to touch the sky, for in the universe there is no terrestrial part higher than its summit; and it is always struck by the rays of the sun in the east four hours before daybreak. Because the mountain is composed of the whitest stone, it shines brilliantly and serves these Armenians <note>original: "Ermini," an archaic term for Armenians</note> much as a beautiful moonlight would in the midst of darkness; and because of its great height, it surpasses the highest reaches of the clouds by a distance of four miles in a straight line. This summit is seen from a great part of the west, illuminated by the sun after its setting until the third part of the night. It is this peak which we, in your company during clear weather, have previously judged to be a comet; and to us, in the darkness of night, it seems to change into various shapes, sometimes dividing into two or three parts, sometimes long and sometimes short; and this arises from the clouds that, on the horiz— <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "orizzonte" (horizon)</note>

Why this comet appears to be of variable shape in such a way that it is now round, now long, and now divided into two or three parts, and now united, and sometimes it disappears, and sometimes it is seen again.

### LETTER III.

Having several times rejoiced with you in letters over your prosperous fortune, I know that now, as a friend, you will grieve with me over the wretched state in which I find myself. It is this: that in recent days I have been in such anxieties, fears, dangers, and losses, together with these miserable villagers, that we had reason to envy the dead. And certainly, I do not believe that since the elements, by their separation, undid the great <term>Chaos</term> <note>In ancient cosmology, Chaos was the formless state of the universe before the elements (earth, air, fire, water) were separated to create order.</note>, they have ever reunited their force—or rather their rage—to do as much harm to men as we have now seen and experienced; so much so that I cannot imagine what more could be added to such an evil as we endured in the space of ten hours.

# FIGURES.

### I. — EXPRESSIVE PAINTING.

Painting, or rather painted figures, must be created in such a way that those who look at them can easily recognize, through their <term>postures</term> <note>original: "attitudini." In Renaissance art theory, this refers to the physical disposition of the body that conveys a specific emotion or action.</note>, the <term>intent of their soul</term> <note>original: "concetto dell' animo." Leonardo believed that a successful painting must manifest the internal "motions of the mind" through external movements.</note>. And if you have to depict a <term>worthy man</term> <note>original: "omo dabbene." A man of honor, character, and social standing.</note> speaking, ensure that his actions are companions to his good words; and similarly, if you have to represent a <term>brutish man</term> <note>original: "omo bestiale." Someone characterized by uncontrolled, animalistic impulses.</note>, do it with fierce movements, throwing his arms toward the listener, and let the head and chest, thrust out beyond the feet, accompany the speaker's hands. This should be done in the likeness of a <term>deaf-mute</term> <note>original: "muto." Leonardo frequently observed those who could not hear or speak to learn how to communicate purely through gesture and facial expression.</note> who, seeing two people speaking—even though he is deprived of <term>hearing</term>—nevertheless understands the theme of their dispute through the effects and the actions of those speakers.

I once saw in Florence a man who had become <term>deaf by accident</term> <note>original: "sordo accidentale." This refers to someone who lost their hearing later in life rather than being born deaf, often implying they still possess the memory of language.</note>, who, if you spoke loudly to him, did not understand you; yet, if you spoke softly, without the sound of the voice, he understood you solely by the movement of the lips. Now you might say to me: "Does a person who speaks loudly not move their lips the same as one who speaks softly? And if the movement is the same, would one not be understood as well as the other?" Regarding this point, I leave the judgment to experience: have someone speak softly and then loudly, and pay close attention to the lips.

## II. — ADVICE FOR THE PAINTER.

Observe in the streets, at the fall of evening, the faces of men and women when the weather is bad; what <term>grace and sweetness</term> <note>original: "grazia e dolcezza." Leonardo frequently advocated for painting in "universal light" (cloudy days or twilight) because harsh shadows obscure the delicate features of the face.</note> can be seen in them!

<margin>2</margin>
## III. — PAINTING MUST SHOW THE PASSION OF THE PAINTED FIGURE.

The good painter has two principal things to paint: that is, the man, and the <term>concept of his mind</term> <note>original: "concetto della mente sua." This is a central tenet of Leonardo’s theory: that the "motions of the mind" (emotions and thoughts) must be visible through the "motions of the body."</note>. The first is easy, the second is difficult, because it must be represented through the gestures and movements of the limbs; and this is to be learned from those who are <term>mute</term> <note>original: "muti." Leonardo suggests that since those who cannot speak rely entirely on physical gestures to convey meaning, they are the ultimate masters of expressive movement for a painter to imitate.</note>, who do it better than any other kind of person.
