## IV. — HOW THE MUTE
## IS THE TEACHER OF THE PAINTER.

The figures of men should have actions appropriate to their activity so that, by seeing them, you understand what they are thinking or saying; these will be well learned by one who imitates the movements of the <term>mute</term> <note>original: "muto." Leonardo often observed the deaf and mute in the streets of Milan and Florence, believing their heightened reliance on gesture provided the purest study of human expression.</note>, who speak with movements of the hands, eyes, eyebrows, and their whole person when they wish to express the <term>concept of their soul</term> <note>original: "concetto dell' animo loro." This refers to the internal emotional or intellectual state—the "motions of the mind"—that the artist must translate into physical form.</note>.
And do not laugh at me because I propose to you a teacher without a tongue to teach you an art that he himself cannot perform; for he will teach you better through deeds than all others can with words. Do not despise such advice, for they are the masters of movement, and they understand from a distance what a person is saying when that person matches the movements of their hands with their words.

## V. — THE VALUE OF PAINTING
## LIES IN THE CORRESPONDENCE OF THE SIGN
## TO THE MEANING.

You shall make figures in such actions as are sufficient to demonstrate what the figure has in its soul; otherwise, your art will not be praiseworthy.

L. DA VINCI.

### VI. — CONTINUATION.

**How a figure is not praiseworthy if there does not appear in it an action which expresses the <term>passion of the soul</term>** <note>original: "passione dell' anima." In Leonardo's time, "passion" referred to any strong emotion or internal state that "moves" the person to action.</note>.

That figure is most praiseworthy which, through its action, best expresses the passion of its mind.

### VII. — INFINITE VARIETY IN THE EXPRESSION OF FEELINGS.

The movements of men are as varied as the variety of <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidenti." Leonardo uses this term to describe external events, sudden occurrences, or changing thoughts that strike the mind and provoke a physical response.</note> that pass through their minds; and each accident moves these men more or less, according to whether they are of greater or lesser power <note>This likely refers to a person's temperament, physical strength, or the intensity of their will.</note> and according to their age, for a young man will make a different motion than an old man when faced with the same situation.

### IX. — ON DEPICTING ONE WHO SPEAKS AMONG MANY PEOPLE.

You should represent the person whom you wish to speak among many people by first considering the subject matter of which he must treat, and then suiting his gestures to that subject. That is: if the subject is <term>persuasive</term> <note>original: "materia persuasiva." Referring to the art of rhetoric, where the speaker aims to convince the audience.</note>, the gestures should be appropriate to that purpose; if the subject is <term>explanatory</term> <note>original: "materia dichiarativa." Where the speaker is laying out logic or "reasons" (ragioni).</note> through various arguments, let the speaker take one finger of the left hand with two fingers of the right, having the two smaller fingers <note>the ring finger and the pinky</note> closed; and with his face turned toward the audience, with his mouth slightly open so that he appears to be speaking; and if he was seated, let it appear that he is...

Another places his hands upon the table and watches; another blows on his morsel; another leans down to see the <term>speaker</term> <note>original: "proponitore." Literally "the proposer" or "the one putting forward the statement," referring here to Christ as he speaks to the group.</note> and shades his eyes with his hand; another pulls back behind the one who is leaning and sees the speaker between the wall and the leaning man.

## XI. — HOW AN ANGRY FIGURE
## SHOULD BE DEPICTED.

For an angry figure, you should make him hold someone by the hair, with their head twisted toward the ground and with one of his knees upon the victim's ribs, while raising his right fist high. This figure should have his hair standing up, his eyebrows low and narrowed, his teeth clenched, and the two corners of his mouth arched downward. His neck should be thick and, because of his leaning toward the enemy, the front of it should be full of <term>wrinkles</term> <note>original: "grinze." Leonardo emphasizes the anatomical distortion caused by intense physical and emotional strain.</note>.

### XII. — HOW TO DEPICT A DESPERATE MAN.

For the desperate man, you should show him stabbing himself with a knife, and with his hands having torn his clothes; let one of these hands be in the act of tearing at the wound itself. You should depict him with feet apart and legs somewhat bent, and his body similarly <term>inclined</term> <note>original: "inverso terra." ### II. — CONCERNING CHILDREN WHO ARE BOUND IN SWADDLING BANDS.

O maritime cities! ### XIV. — OF THE LANGUAGES OF VARIOUS PEOPLES.

The human race will come to such a pass that the speech of one will not be understood by another—that is, a German with a Turk. <note>Leonardo presents the existence of different languages as a "prophecy" of future confusion, though he is likely making a dry observation about the lack of a universal tongue.</note>

### XV. — OF SOLDIERS ON HORSEBACK.

Many shall be seen carried by great animals, at a swift pace, to the ruin of their lives and most rapid death. Through the air and over the earth, animals of various colors will be seen carrying men with fury to the destruction of their lives. <note>Leonardo describes the violence of cavalry charges. The "animals of various colors" are horses, and the "ruin" refers to the carnage of the battlefield.</note>

### XVI. — OF SAWYERS.

There will be many who will move one against the other, holding a sharp iron blade in their hands; these will do no other harm to each other than that of exhaustion, for as much as one pushes forward, the other retreats back. But woe to him who intervenes between them, for in the end, he will remain cut into pieces. <note>This is a riddle describing two men using a large, two-handled crosscut saw. The "fighting" is actually the rhythmic back-and-forth motion of their work.</note>

### XVII. — OF DIGGERS.

Many will be those who, flaying their mother, will turn her skin inside out—the workers of the earth. <note>In this riddle, "the mother" is the Earth (Mother Earth). To "flay her and turn her skin inside out" is a metaphor for plowing or digging the soil to prepare it for planting.</note>

Men will see with pleasure the undoing and breaking of their own works. <note>In the craft of shoemaking or leatherworking, the artisan must cut and tear at the hides—his materials—to create the finished product.</note>

### XXI. — OF THE MOWING OF GRASS.

Innumerable lives will be extinguished, and innumerable holes will be made upon the earth. <note>This refers to the harvest or the scything of a meadow. The "lives" are the individual plants or blades of grass being cut down.</note>

### XXII. — OF GRAIN AND OTHER SEEDS.

Men will throw out of their own houses those provisions which were dedicated to sustaining their lives. <note>Like the earlier riddle on sowing, this highlights the irony of the farmer casting away the very grain intended for his survival, trusting that it will return as a harvest.</note>

### XXIII. — ON THE THRESHING OF GRAIN.

Men will cruelly beat that which is the cause of their very life — <note>original: "batteranno il grano"</note> threshing the grain. <note>Leonardo is describing the harvest process where the wheat is struck with a flail to separate the edible grain from the husk. To an observer unaware of the context, it looks like a violent assault on the source of human sustenance.</note>

### XXIV. — OF THE PLAYERS.

The skins of animals will rouse men from their silence with loud shouts and curses — <note>original: "le balle da giuocare"</note> playing balls. <note>In the Renaissance, balls for games were often made of leather or animal bladders. Leonardo notes the irony that these animal remains are what trigger the boisterous and often profane behavior of sportsmen.</note>

### XXV. — OF THE SOUND OF THE BAGPIPES.

The wind, passing through the skins of animals, will make men leap — that is, the bagpipes, which cause dancing. <note>The bagpipe, or "piva," is made from an animal hide bag. Leonardo describes the music not as art, but as a physical phenomenon of wind forcing a physical reaction—dancing—from the listeners.</note>

### XXVI. — OF DICE.

The bones of the dead will be seen, in swift motion, deciding the fortune of the one who moves them — the dice. <note>Because dice were commonly carved from animal bone, Leonardo presents the game of craps or hazard as a morbid ritual where the "dead" control the destiny of the living.</note>

### XXVII. — OF THE FLOGGED AND BEATEN.

Men will hide themselves under the rinds of stripped plants, and there, crying out, will inflict martyrdom upon themselves, with the beating of their own limbs. <note>This riddle refers to the processing of flax or hemp to make linen. The "stripped plants" are the fibers worn as clothing, and the "beating" refers to the rhythmic strikes used in textile production or, metaphorically, to the self-flagellation of religious penitents who wore linen shirts.</note>

### XXVIII. — THE TONGUES OF PIGS AND CALVES IN THE INTESTINES.

Oh! what a filthy thing, for it will be seen that one animal has its tongue in the backside of another. <note>original: "la lingua in culo all' altro." Leonardo is describing the making of sausages or cured meats, where various pieces of meat—including tongues—are stuffed into intestinal casings. What is a common culinary practice is presented here as a grotesque anatomical paradox.</note>

### XXIX. — OF PEASANTS WORKING IN THEIR SHIRTS.

Darkness will come from the midst of the East, which will stain the sky covering Italy with such great obscurity. <note>original: "Verranno tenebre in mezzo l' Oriente." This likely refers to the clouds of dust or chaff kicked up by peasants during the winnowing of grain, or perhaps the soot from clearing fields by fire. To the observer, the labor creates a localized "eclipse" or "darkness."</note>

### XXX. — OF BARBERS.

All men will flee to Africa. <note>This is one of Leonardo’s clever puns. In the Renaissance, "Africa" was often used as a metaphor for darkness or "the land of the Moors." Leonardo suggests that as the barber shaves a man or cuts his dark hair, the hair "fleeing" the head or the transformation of the man’s appearance is a journey into this metaphorical darkness.</note>

## THE PROPHECIES
## OF IRRATIONAL ANIMALS.

---

### I. — THEY PULL THE CANNONS.

Oxen will be, in large part, the cause of the destruction of cities, and likewise horses and buffalo. <note>original: "Tiran le bombarde." Leonardo refers to the draft animals used to haul heavy artillery (bombards) and siege engines to the battlefield. Though the animals are "irrational" and innocent, their strength is the primary engine of urban ruin during war.</note>

### II. — OF THE OXEN THAT ARE EATEN.

The masters of the estates will eat their own workers. <note>original: "Mangeranno i padron delle possessioni i lor propri lavoratori." In this social riddle, the "workers" are the oxen who labor in the fields. Leonardo highlights the irony and perceived cruelty of a landowner slaughtering and consuming the very animal that performed the labor to provide his wealth.</note>

### III. — OF BEATEN DONKEYS.

O neglected nature, why have you become partial, making yourself a compassionate and kind mother to some of your children, and to others a most cruel and heartless stepmother? I see your children being given into the servitude of others, without ever receiving any benefit; and in place of reward for the good they have done, they are paid with the greatest torments; and they spend their whole lives for the benefit of their mistreaters. <note>original: "suo malefattore." Leonardo often wrote about the cruelty of man toward animals. Here, he personifies Nature to ask why some creatures are born to suffer while others live in ease.</note>

### IV. — OF DONKEYS.

Their many labors will be rewarded with hunger, thirst, hardship, blows, prods, curses, and great insults.

### V. — OF THE BELLS OF MULES WHICH ARE CLOSE TO THEIR EARS.

In many parts of Europe, instruments of various sizes will be heard making diverse harmonies, causing the greatest hardship to those who hear them most closely. <note>Leonardo is describing the bells attached to the harnesses of pack animals. While the "harmony" of the bells might be pleasant to a passerby, it is a constant, deafening "hardship" for the mule whose ears are right next to the metal.</note>

### VI. — OF MULES THAT CARRY RICH LOADS OF SILVER AND GOLD.

Many treasures and great riches will be placed upon four-footed animals, who will carry them to various places. <note>This "prophecy" points out the irony of the Renaissance economy: the most valuable materials in the world—gold and silver—are hauled through the mud by animals who receive nothing but heavy burdens for their trouble.</note>

<summary>In these riddles, Leonardo laments the cruel treatment of beasts of burden, particularly donkeys and mules, contrasting their hard labor and the wealth they carry with the hunger and violence they receive in return.</summary>

## VII. — OF KID-GOATS.

The time of Herod shall return, for innocent children shall be taken from their nurses, and shall die of great wounds at the hands of cruel men. <note>original: "Ritornerà il tempo d’Erode." Leonardo uses the biblical Massacre of the Innocents as a metaphor for the slaughter of young goats (kids) for their meat.</note>

## VIII. — OF SHEEP, COWS, GOATS, AND THE LIKE.

From countless mothers, their small children shall be taken, and these shall be slaughtered and most cruelly quartered.

## IX. — OF CATS THAT EAT MICE.

To you, cities of Africa! Your children shall be seen torn apart in their own homes by most cruel and rapacious animals of your own country. <note>Leonardo often framed his riddles as if they were prophecies for distant lands like Africa or Turkey to add an air of mystery, though he is simply describing a cat catching a mouse.</note>

## X. — THE BEES THAT MAKE THE WAX FOR CANDLES.

He who creates the light for divine worship shall be drowned. <note>Leonardo refers to the practice of killing or "drowning" bees (often with smoke or water) to harvest their wax, which was then used to make candles for church altars.</note>
And those who feed on grass shall turn night into day — tallow. <note>original: "sevo." Tallow is rendered animal fat from cattle or sheep (grazers); it was the primary material for cheap candles used to light homes at night.</note>

## XI. — OF BEES.

And from many others, their provisions and their food shall be taken, and they shall be cruelly treated by people without... <note>The text breaks off here; Leonardo is describing the harvesting of honey, where the bees' winter "provisions" are stolen by humans.</note>

### XII. — OF ANTS.

Many shall be the peoples who will hide themselves, their children, and their provisions within dark caverns; and there, in those gloomy places, they shall feed themselves and their families for many months, without any other light, whether artificial or natural. <note>Leonardo describes the life of an ant colony underground during the winter months.</note>

### XIII. — OF FLIES AND OTHER INSECTS.

Men shall come out of their graves, transformed into birds, and they shall attack other men, snatching the food from their very hands and tables — flies. <note>This riddle plays on the life cycle of flies, which often emerge from decaying matter (the "graves") and fly about like tiny birds to pester humans during meals.</note>

### XIV. — OF OWLS OR LITTLE OWLS USED TO HUNT WITH BIRD-LIME.

Many shall perish with their heads shattered, and their eyes shall pop out from much of their heads, because of fearful animals emerged from the darkness. <note>original: "civette o gufi con che s' uccella alla pania." This refers to a historical hunting technique where a tethered owl was used to lure smaller birds into "bird-lime" (a sticky adhesive on branches); the hunter would then kill the trapped birds by crushing their heads.</note>

### XV. — OF SNAKES CARRIED BY STORKS.

Long serpents shall be seen in the great heights of the air, fighting with birds. <note>Leonardo observes the natural sight of a stork or predatory bird catching a snake and carrying it into the sky as the snake struggles to free itself.</note>

# THE PROPHECIES OF PLANTS.

---

## I. — OF WALNUTS AND OLIVES
### AND ACORNS AND CHESTNUTS AND THE LIKE.

Many children shall be snatched from the very arms of their mothers by pitiless beatings, thrown to the ground, and then torn apart. <note>A riddle describing the harvest: the fruit (children) are knocked off the trees (mothers) with long poles.</note>

## II. — OF BEATEN WALNUT TREES.

Those who have done the best shall be the most beaten, and their children taken and flayed <note>original: "scorticati," referring to the removal of the outer green husk.</note>, or rather stripped, and their bones broken and crushed. <note>Leonardo observes the irony that the most productive walnut tree receives the most blows from the harvester’s pole; the "broken bones" are the cracked shells of the nuts.</note>

### III. — OF OLIVES THAT FALL FROM THE OLIVE TREES, GIVING US OIL FOR LIGHT.

They shall descend with fury toward the earth
and shall give us nourishment and light.

The trees and shrubs of the great forests shall be

Fathers and mothers shall be seen to provide much
more benefit to stepchildren than to their own true
children.
<note>In this riddle, the "parents" are the original trees, the "true children" are their own natural fruit, and the "stepchildren" are the foreign branches grafted onto them which receive the tree's sap.</note>

### II. — OF SIEVES MADE OF ANIMAL SKINS.

One shall see the food of animals pass through their skins in every part, except for the mouth, and penetrate from the opposite side down to the level ground.
<note>Leonardo refers to grain (animal fodder) being sifted through a sieve made of perforated leather.</note>

### III. — OF LANTERNS.

The fierce horns of powerful bulls shall defend the light of the night from the impetuous fury of the winds.
<note>In the Renaissance, before glass was cheap and common, lanterns used thin, translucent shavings of animal horn to protect the candle flame.</note>

### IV. — OF THE SAME.

Oxen, with their horns, shall defend the fire from its death—the lantern.

### V. — OF THE HANDLES OF KNIVES MADE FROM THE HORNS OF RAMS.

In the horns of animals shall be seen sharp irons, with which the lives of many of their own kind are taken.
<note>A riddle describing knives with horn handles used by butchers to slaughter livestock.</note>

### VI. — OF BOWS MADE WITH THE HORNS OF OXEN.

Many shall be those who, because of bovine horns, shall die a painful death.
<note>This refers to composite bows, which were constructed using layers of wood, sinew, and horn to increase their power and range in warfare.</note>

### VII. — OF FEATHERS IN BEDS.

Winged creatures shall support men with their own feathers.
<note>Leonardo refers to feather-stuffed mattresses and pillows, which allow people to sleep supported by the plumage of birds.</note>

### VIII. — OF THE REED IN THE LOOM.

Oftentimes, that which is divided shall be the cause of great union — that is, the reed, made of divided cane, unites the threads of the silk.
<note>The "pettine" or reed of a loom is a frame with many thin, separated slats (originally made of cane). Although the slats are separate, they work together to push the weft threads together, creating a unified fabric.</note>

### IX. — THE SILK-SPINNING WHEEL.

One shall hear mournful cries, piercing shrieks, and hoarse, fiery voices of those who are stripped with torment and finally left naked and motionless; and this shall happen because of the motor that turns everything.
<note>This "prophecy" describes the processing of silk. The "shrieks" are the sounds of the spinning machinery, and those being "stripped" are the silkworms or cocoons, which are unwound until the pupa inside is left bare.</note>

### X. — OF FLAX WHICH TREATS THE AILMENTS OF PEOPLE.

The precepts of one who was first bound, laid out, and martyred by many various beatings shall be revered, honored, and listened to with reverence and love.
<note>Leonardo refers to the processing of flax to make linen or paper. The plant is "beaten" (scutched) to extract fibers. The "precepts" likely refer to the laws or scriptures written upon paper made from linen rags, or perhaps the use of linen for sacred vestments.</note>

### XI. — OF THE HANDLE OF THE AXE.

The forests shall give birth to sons who will be the cause of their own death — the handle of the axe.
<note>A classic riddle: the wooden handle of an axe is a "son" of the forest, yet it is the tool that allows the axe-head to chop down the trees.</note>

### XII. — THE STICK WHICH IS DEAD.
<note>original: "IL BASTONE CH'È MORTO"</note>

The movement of the dead shall make many of the living flee with pain, weeping, and cries.
<note>In Leonardo’s riddles, wood is often called "the dead" because it is no longer a living tree. Here, he refers to a wooden stick or club used to beat people, causing them to flee in pain.</note>

### XIII. — OF SNARES AND TRAPS.
<note>original: "DE' LACCIUOLI E TRAPPOLE"</note>

Many dead things shall move with fury, and shall seize and bind the living, and shall serve their enemies toward their death and destruction.
<note>The "dead things" are the wooden components or fibers of a trap. Though inanimate, they "move with fury" when the mechanism is triggered, catching living animals for the benefit of the hunter—the "enemy."</note>

### XIV. — OF THE MOTION OF WATERS THAT CARRY TIMBERS WHICH ARE DEAD.
<note>original: "DEL MOTO DELL'ACQUE CHE PORTANO I LEGNAMI CHE SON MORTI"</note>

Bodies without souls shall move of their own accord, and shall carry with them an innumerable generation of the dead, taking away the riches of the surrounding living.
<note>Leonardo describes wooden ships or rafts (the "bodies without souls") floating on a river current. They transport vast quantities of timber (the "generation of the dead"). The "taking of riches" likely refers to the trade and tolls associated with river commerce, or perhaps the way a flood strips the wealth of the land.</note>

### XV. — OF CARTS AND SHIPS.
<note>original: "DEI CARRI E NAVI"</note>

The dead shall be seen carrying the living — carts and ships in various parts.
<note>This is a classic Leonardo paradox: the "dead" wood of the cart or the vessel provides the means of transport for living humans.</note>

### XVI. — OF THE CHESTS THAT ENCLOSE MANY TREASURES.
<note>original: "DELLE CASSE CHE RISERRANO MOLTI TESORI"</note>

Within walnuts and trees and other plants shall be found very great treasures, which lie hidden there and well guarded.
<note>The "chests" are the shells of nuts or the trunks of trees. The "treasures" are the nourishing seeds (like the walnut meat) or the valuable timber found within the plant.</note>

### XVII. — OF NAVIGATION.
<note>original: "DEL NAVIGARE"</note>

The trees of the great forests of Taurus and Sinai, the Apennines and Atlas, shall be seen rushing through the air from East to West, and from North to South; and they shall carry through the air a vast multitude of men.
<note>Leonardo uses "the trees" to refer to the timber used to build ships. They "rush through the air" because their masts and sails are propelled by the wind. To a person of the Renaissance, the idea of forests crossing the sea was a powerful image of global expansion.</note>
Oh! how many vows! Oh! how many dead! Oh! how many separations of friends and kin! And how many shall there be who will never again see their own provinces or their homelands, and who shall die without burial, with their bones scattered in diverse places of the world!

### XVIII. — OF NAVIGATION.
<note>original: "DEL NAVIGARE"</note>

There shall be great winds, by which things of the East shall become things of the West; and those of the South, largely mingled with the course of the winds, shall follow them through distant lands.
<note>This refers to the global trade of spices, silks, and other goods moved by sailing ships across the oceans.</note>

### XIX. — OF SHIPS THAT SINK.
<note>original: "DE' NAVILI CHE ANNEGANO"</note>

Vast bodies, without life, shall be seen carrying a multitude of men with fury to the destruction of their lives.
<note>The "bodies without life" are the wooden hulls of ships, which, when caught in a storm or wrecked, lead to the "destruction" (death) of the sailors on board.</note>

### XX. — OF ANIMALS THAT GO UPON THE EARTH WEARING CLOGS.
<note>original: "LI ANIMALI CHE VAN SOPRA LE TERRE ANDANDO IN ZOCCOLO"</note>

The mud shall be so deep that men shall walk upon the trees of their own lands.
<note>This is a clever riddle. The "trees" are the wood used to make <term>zoccoli</term> (wooden-soled clogs or pattens). By wearing these shoes to keep their feet out of the mud, men are literally walking "upon trees."</note>

<summary>Leonardo uses the metaphor of "dead" timber to describe the wonders and tragedies of sea travel, ending with a riddle about men walking on trees to avoid mud—a reference to wooden clogs.</summary>

### XXI. — OF WINE-SKINS.*
<note>original: "DELLE BAGHE"</note>

Goats shall carry the wine to the cities.
<note>Leonardo refers to the fact that wine was commonly transported in bags made from goat hides.</note>

### XXII. — OF THE SUNSHADE.
<note>original: "DEL PARASOLE"</note>

The striking of the sun’s sphere shall appear to be such that he who believes he is covering it shall instead be covered by it.
<note>A person holding a parasol (sunshade) intends to "cover" the sun to block its light, but the result is that the person is covered by the shade of the parasol.</note>

## II.

### I. — OF STONES TURNED INTO LIME FROM WHICH PRISONS ARE BUILT.
<note>original: "DE' SASSI CONVERTITI IN CALCINA..."</note>

Many things that shall be undone by fire before this time shall take away the liberty of many men.
<note>This describes the process of making mortar. Limestone is "undone by fire" in a kiln to create lime (calcina), which is then used to build the stone walls of prisons that hold men captive.</note>

### II. — OF THE REFLECTION OF CITY WALLS IN THE WATER OF THEIR MOATS.
<note>original: "DELLO SPECCHIARE LE MURA..."</note>

The high walls of great cities shall be seen upside down in their moats.

### III. — OF OVENS.
<note>original: "DEI FORNI"</note>

Food shall be taken from the mouths of many — at the ovens.
<note>This riddle plays on the act of putting unbaked dough into an oven (the "mouth") to be cooked; the bread is "taken away" from the person's immediate reach to be baked.</note>

### IV. — AGAIN OF OVENS.

To those who are fed by the hands of others, the food shall be taken from their mouths — the oven.
<note>Leonardo refers to the baker using a wooden shovel (a peel) to place dough into the "mouth" of the oven. The oven "takes" the food to bake it.</note>

### V. — OF PUTTING AND TAKING BREAD FROM THE MOUTH OF THE OVEN.

Throughout all cities, lands, castles, and houses, one shall see—out of a desire to eat—the snatching of one's own food from the mouth of another, without the latter being able to offer any defense.
<note>In this riddle, the "mouth of another" is the oven's opening. The "defense" is impossible because the oven is an inanimate object.</note>

### VI. — OF BRICK AND LIME KILNS.

In the end, the earth shall turn red from the firing of many days, and stones shall be converted into ashes.
<note>This describes industrial processes: clay (earth) turns red when fired into bricks, and limestone is burned in a kiln to create lime, which resembles white ash.</note>

### VII. — OF WEAPONS OF OFFENSE.

The works of human hands shall be the cause of their own death — swords and spears.

### VIII. — IRON TAKEN FROM UNDER THE EARTH IS DEAD, AND OF IT ARE MADE THE WEAPONS THAT HAVE KILLED SO MANY MEN.

The dead shall come out from under the earth, and with their fierce movements, they shall drive innumerable human creatures from the world.
<note>Leonardo characterizes iron ore as "dead" because it is inanimate matter from underground. Once forged into swords and moved "fiercely" by soldiers, it causes the death of the living.</note>

### IX. — OF SWORDS AND SPEARS
### WHICH BY THEMSELVES NEVER HARM ANYONE.

He who by nature is gentle, and without any offense, will become terrifying and fierce through evil company, and will take the lives of many people most cruelly; and he would kill even more, if bodies without souls, coming out of caves, did not defend them — that is, iron armor.
<note>In this riddle, the "gentle" character is the iron itself, which is harmless until held by the "evil company" of a soldier. The "bodies without souls" are suits of plate armor, forged from metal taken from mines (caves), which protect the victims from the weapons.</note>

### X. — OF THE STARS OF THE SPURS.

Because of the stars, men shall be seen to be most swift, equal to any fast animal.
<note>The "stars" are the rowels—the spiked, star-shaped wheels—on a rider's spurs. By pricking the horse, the rider can match the speed of the fastest animals.</note>

### XI. — OF THE FIRE OF THE CANNONS.

Oh! how many great buildings shall be ruined because of fire!

### XII. — OF THE CANNONS
### THAT COME OUT OF THE PIT AND THE MOLD.

There shall come from under the earth that which, with terrifying cries, shall stun those nearby, and with its breath shall cause men to die, and cities and castles to be ruined.
<note>Leonardo describes the birth and use of a "bombard" (a heavy cannon). In the Renaissance, these were cast in bronze or iron within a "form" (mold) buried in a casting pit. The "cries" are the roar of the blast, and the "breath" is the lethal force of the gunpowder explosion.</note>

Simple folk shall carry a great quantity of lights to light the way for all those who have completely lost the power of vision.
<note>This is a riddle describing a funeral procession. The "simple folk" are the mourners carrying candles, and those who have "lost the power of vision" are the dead in their coffins.</note>

## III. — OF ALL SOULS’ DAY.

And how many shall there be who will weep for their dead ancestors, bringing lights to them.
<note>Leonardo refers to the tradition of lighting candles and lamps at the graves of the deceased on All Souls' Day (November 2nd).</note>

## IV. — OF THE LAMENTATION PERFORMED ON GOOD FRIDAY.

In all parts of Europe there shall be weeping by great peoples for the death of a single man, who died in the East.
<note>This riddle describes the liturgical mourning for Jesus Christ during Holy Week. The "man who died in the East" is Jesus, crucified in Jerusalem.</note>

## V. — OF CHRISTIANS.

Many, who hold the faith of the Son, build temples only in the name of the Mother.
<note>Leonardo is observing the prevalence of churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary (the Mother) relative to those dedicated specifically to Christ (the Son).</note>

## VI. — OF THE CENSER OF INCENSE.

Those who, in white vestments, shall go with arrogant movements threatening with metal and fire those who did them no harm.
<note>Leonardo describes the priest or thurifer swinging a metal censer containing hot coals and incense. To an observer unaware of the ritual, the swinging of a heavy metal object with fire inside might appear as a threatening gesture.</note>

## VII. — OF PRIESTS WHO SAY MASS.

Many shall be those who, to practice their art, will dress themselves most richly: and this shall seem to be done according to the custom of wearing aprons.
<note>Leonardo compares the elaborate liturgical vestments (like the chasuble) to the protective aprons worn by craftsmen, suggesting that the clergy are "craftsmen" of the ritual.</note>

### IX. — OF THE CONFESSOR FRIARS.

Unfortunate women, of their own free will, shall go to reveal to men all their lusts and their shameful and most secret deeds.
<note>Leonardo frames the Sacrament of Penance (Confession) as a strange social phenomenon where private "shames" are voluntarily disclosed to strangers (the clergy).</note>

### X. — OF ADORED PAINTINGS OF SAINTS.

Men shall speak to men who do not hear; they shall have their eyes open and not see; they shall speak to them and receive no answer; they shall ask grace of those who have ears and do not hear; they shall carry lights for those who are blind.
<note>This riddle describes the act of praying to religious icons and statues. To an outsider, the devotee appears to be talking to a deaf and blind object while lighting candles for a "person" (the statue) who cannot see the light.</note>

### XI. — OF SCULPTURES.

Alas! I see the Savior crucified once more.
<note>Leonardo refers to the physical act of a sculptor carving or casting a crucifix—an "imitation" of the crucifixion performed for art or commerce.</note>

### XII. — OF CRUCIFIXES THAT ARE SOLD.

I see Christ sold and crucified once more, and his saints martyred.
<note>A sharp critique of the sale of religious objects and relics. By selling a representation of Christ, Leonardo suggests the merchants are repeating the betrayal of Judas and the violence of the executioners.</note>

### XIII. — OF THE RELIGION OF THE FRIARS WHO LIVE BY THEIR SAINTS, WHO HAVE BEEN DEAD FOR A LONG TIME!

Those who are dead, after a thousand years, shall be the ones who pay the expenses of many of the living.
<note>Leonardo is commenting on the wealth of the Church and monastic orders, which was often sustained by the veneration of long-dead saints through pilgrimages, offerings, and the sale of indulgences.</note>

<header>THE PROPHECIES.</header>

### XIV. — ON THE SELLING OF PARADISE.

An infinite multitude shall publicly and peacefully sell things of the highest price, without the permission of the owner of those things, and which never belonged to them, nor were they ever in their power; and to this, human justice shall provide no remedy.
<note>Leonardo is referring to the sale of indulgences—the practice of paying the Church for the remission of temporal punishment for sins. The "owner" is God, and the "things of highest price" are the entry to Paradise, which Leonardo argues the clergy have no right to sell.</note>

### XV. — OF FRIARS WHO, BY SPENDING WORDS, RECEIVE GREAT RICHES AND GIVE AWAY PARADISE.

Invisible coins shall cause many who spend them to triumph.
<note>The "invisible coins" are the promises of spiritual rewards, prayers, and blessings. Leonardo satirizes how friars "spend" these intangible promises in exchange for very real, material wealth and influence.</note>

### XVI. — OF CHURCHES AND THE DWELLINGS OF FRIARS.

There shall be many who will abandon their spiritual exercises, their labors, and their poverty of life and possessions, and will go to dwell within riches and magnificent buildings, claiming that this is the means of making oneself a friend to God.
<note>This is a critique of the "Mendicant" orders (like the Franciscans or Dominicans) who were founded on principles of extreme poverty but, by Leonardo's time, had commissioned some of the most "triumphant" and expensive architecture in Italy.</note>

<summary>In these riddles, Leonardo delivers a biting satire of the Catholic Church, focusing on the sale of indulgences, the accumulation of wealth through spiritual promises, and the hypocrisy of friars living in luxury.</summary>

## THE PROPHECIES OF SOCIAL CUSTOMS.

---

### I. — ON MOVING OUT ON ALL SAINTS' DAY.

Many will abandon their own dwellings and carry their <term>possessions<note>original: "valsenti", meaning one's wealth, property, or belongings.</note></term> with them, and go to inhabit other lands.
<note>In Leonardo’s time, it was a common custom to end house leases and move to new lodgings on All Saints' Day (November 1st). He describes this routine chore as if it were a mass migration or exile.</note>

### II. — OF MEN WHO SLEEP WITHIN THE PLANKS OF TREES.

Men shall sleep, and eat, and dwell within trees that were born in the forests and fields.
<note>The solution to this riddle is the wooden bed or perhaps a wooden house. Leonardo is describing the transformation of timber into furniture or shelter.</note>

### III. — OF BEATING THE BED TO REMAKE IT.

Men shall reach such a state of ingratitude that he who gives them lodging, without any cost, shall be loaded with blows, in such a manner that a great part of his internal organs will be displaced from their position and go tumbling through his body.
<note>This refers to the act of fluffing a wool or feather mattress. The "lodging" is the bed itself; the "blows" are the person beating the mattress to soften it; the "internal organs" are the stuffing (wool, straw, or feathers) being tossed around inside the fabric casing.</note>

### IV. — THE DOCTORS WHO LIVE OFF THE SICK.

Men will fall into such <term>lowliness<note>original: "viltà", suggesting a loss of dignity or a wretched state.</note></term> that they will be grateful that others should triumph over...
<note>The original text cuts off here, but Leonardo is beginning a critique of the medical profession. He often viewed doctors of his time as parasites who profited from the suffering and physical decline of their fellow men.</note>

---

### V. — OF THE COMMON PEOPLE.

## THE PROPHECIES OF THINGS
## WHICH ARE IMPOSSIBLE IN NATURE.

---

### I. — OF THE PIT.

Many will be busily occupied in the labor of taking away from that thing which grows the more, the more is taken from it.
<note>The solution to this riddle is a hole or a pit (fossa). As you remove dirt, the hole itself increases in size.</note>

### II. — OF THE WEIGHT PLACED UPON THE FEATHER CUSHION.

And many bodies, when they see their heads removed, will be seen to grow visibly.
<note>The "body" is a feather pillow or cushion (piumaccio). When the "head" of the sleeper is lifted off it, the compressed feathers spring back, and the pillow expands.</note>

...and, upon returning the lifted head to them, they immediately decrease in size.
<note>This completes the riddle from the previous page regarding a feather pillow (piumaccio). The "body" of the pillow grows when the sleeper’s head is removed and shrinks when the head is replaced.</note>

### III. — OF THE CATCHING OF LICE.

There shall be many hunters of animals who, the more they catch, the fewer they will have; and conversely, they will have the more, the fewer they catch.
<note>The "hunters" are people picking lice or parasites from themselves; if they catch the insects, they discard them (thus having fewer on their bodies), but if they fail to catch them, they remain infested (having more).</note>

### IV. — OF DRAWING WATER WITH TWO BUCKETS ON A SINGLE ROPE.

And many shall be kept busy who, the more they pull the thing downward, the more it will flee in the opposite direction.
<note>This describes a well with a pulley system. As you pull one end of the rope down to raise a bucket, the bucket on the other end of the rope (the "thing") moves away from you in the opposite direction.</note>

### I. — OF THE MISER.

Many shall be those who, with all zeal and diligence, will furiously pursue that thing which has always terrified them, not knowing its <term>malice<note>original: "malignità".</note></term>.
<note>Leonardo is likely referring to gold or wealth. The "miser" pursues riches with frantic energy, even though the consequences of greed—fear of loss, spiritual decay, or social isolation—are things that would normally terrify a person.</note>

### II. — OF MEN WHO, THE OLDER THEY GROW, THE MORE MISERLY THEY BECOME, FOR HAVING LITTLE TIME LEFT THEY OUGHT TO BE MORE GENEROUS.

Those who are judged to have the most experience and judgment shall be seen seeking and searching with the greatest greed for things, even as they have the least need for them.
<note>Leonardo highlights the irony of elderly misers who hoard wealth they will never live to spend.</note>

### III. — OF THE DESIRE FOR WEALTH.

Men shall pursue that thing which they most fear; that is, they will live in misery so as not to fall into misery.
<note>The "thing they most fear" is poverty (misery). To avoid it, they live like paupers to save money, thus creating the very state of "misery" they intended to escape.</note>

### IV. — OF THINGS WHICH ARE EATEN, WHICH ARE FIRST KILLED.

Their nourisher will be killed by them, and scourged with a pitiless death.
<note>This refers to livestock and animals raised for food; humans kill the very creatures that provide them with sustenance.</note>

### V. — OF THE MOUTH OF MAN, WHICH IS A TOMB.

Great noises shall issue from the tombs of those who have died a wretched and violent death.
<note>This is a riddle for eating meat. The "tomb" is the human mouth or stomach, and the "noises" are the sounds of chewing or perhaps the cries of the living who consume the dead.</note>

A great part of living bodies shall pass through the bodies of other animals; that is, the houses of—
<note>The "houses" here refers to the bodies of the consumers. The sentence is interrupted by the page break.</note>

### VII. — OF THE LIFE OF MEN WHO CHANGE THEIR FLESH EVERY YEAR.

Men shall pass, dead, through their own bowels.
<note>This is a scientific observation disguised as a riddle. Leonardo understood that the human body is constantly renewing itself; as old tissue dies and is expelled, the "dead" man passes through his own digestive system.</note>

### VIII. — OF THE CRUELTY OF MAN.

There shall be seen upon the earth creatures who will always be at war with one another, with very great losses and frequent deaths on each side.

These shall have no limit to their malice; by their fierce limbs, a great part of the trees of the vast forests of the universe shall be brought to the ground; and once they have fed, the nourishment of their desires shall be to deal death and affliction, labors, wars, and furies to every living thing. And through their boundless pride, these will wish to rise toward the heavens, but the excessive weight of their limbs shall keep them down. Nothing shall remain above the earth, or under the earth and water, that is not per—
<note>This famous passage is a scathing critique of humanity. Leonardo describes humans as the most cruel of "animals," noting our capacity for deforestation and our relentless drive to destroy other living things for sport or power rather than just for hunger.</note>

### IX. — OF THE READING OF GOOD BOOKS.

Happy shall be those who lend their ears to the words of the dead: — to read good works, and to observe them.
<note>In this riddle, the "words of the dead" are books written by authors who have long since passed away. Leonardo suggests that true happiness and wisdom come from studying the enduring legacy of past thinkers.</note>

### X. — OF BOOKS WHICH TEACH PRECEPTS.

Bodies without souls shall give us, through their maxims, precepts useful for dying well.
<note>The "bodies without souls" are books (often made of leather or parchment). The "well-dying" refers to the historical tradition of *Ars Moriendi*, or the art of living a virtuous life so as to meet death with a clear conscience.</note>

### XI. — OF FAME.

Feathers shall lift men, just like birds, toward the heavens: — that is, through the letters written by those pens.
<note>Leonardo plays on the double meaning of the Italian word *penne*, which means both "feathers" (enabling flight) and "quill pens" (enabling writing). It is through writing that a person's name and fame reach the heights of the "heavens."</note>

### XII. — OF THE SKINS OF ANIMALS WHICH RETAIN THE SENSE OF TOUCH, WHICH IS UPON THE WRITINGS.

The more one speaks with skins, the garments of sensation, the more wisdom shall be acquired.
<note>Parchment and vellum were made from animal skins. Leonardo refers to these as the "garments of sensation" because skin is the organ of touch. This riddle explains that by "speaking" with these skins—that is, by reading books—one gains knowledge.</note>

### XIII. — OF HISTORY.

Disunited things shall be united, and shall receive within themselves such virtue that they will restore to men their lost memory: — that is, the papyri <note>original: "papiri." While Leonardo says papyrus, he is referring to paper in general.</note> which are made of disunited hairs <note>Leonardo refers to the plant fibers or shredded rags used in paper-making as "hairs."</note>, and hold the memory of the things and deeds of men.

### XIV. — AT EVERY POINT ON EARTH, A DIVISION OF TWO HEMISPHERES CAN BE MADE.

All men will instantly change their hemisphere.
<note>This is a geographical riddle. Since the line dividing East and West or North and South can be drawn anywhere, a person "changes hemispheres" simply by taking a single step or shifting their position relative to an imaginary line.</note>

### XV. — AT EVERY POINT THERE IS A DIVISION FROM EAST TO WEST.

All animals will move from the East to the West, and likewise from the North <note>original: "aquilone," referring to the North Wind.</note> to the South <note>original: "meriggio," literally "midday," the direction of the sun at its zenith.</note> interchangeably, and so conversely.

### XVI. — OF THE HEMISPHERES, WHICH ARE INFINITE AND DIVIDED BY INFINITE LINES, SO THAT EVERY MAN ALWAYS HAS ONE OF THESE LINES BETWEEN ONE FOOT AND THE OTHER.

Men will speak, and touch, and embrace each other, while standing in one hemisphere or the other, and they will understand each other's languages.
<note>Leonardo is playing with the mathematical concept of the horizon and the meridian. Because these lines are everywhere, two people can be close enough to touch while technically being separated by the "line" that divides the world into two halves.</note>

### XVII. — OF THE CLOUDS.

A great part of the sea will flee toward the sky and for a long time will not return: — that is, by means of the clouds.
<note>Leonardo is describing the water cycle. To a listener expecting a miracle, "the sea fleeing to heaven" sounds supernatural, but it is simply evaporation forming clouds.</note>

### XVIII. — SNOWFALL, <br> WHICH IS WATER.

Water fallen from the clouds, while still in motion upon the slopes <note>original: "spiagge," which can mean shores or slopes; in the context of mountains, it refers to the mountain sides.</note> of mountains, will come to a halt for a long period of time without making any movement, and this will happen in many and diverse provinces.
<note>The "halted water" is snow or ice, which remains frozen on the mountainside throughout the winter.</note>

### XIX. — THE SNOWBALL <br> ROLLING UPON THE SNOW.

Many will be those who shall grow in their own ruins.
<note>This is a clever play on words. As a snowball rolls down a hill, it is technically "falling" or "going to ruin," yet it increases in size by gathering more snow as it descends.</note>

### XX. — OF RAINS, <br> WHICH CAUSE TURBID RIVERS <br> TO CARRY AWAY THE EARTH.

The sky will become so changed that it will transpose a great part of Africa, which reveals itself to that sky, toward Europe, and those of Europe toward Africa; and those of the Scythian <note>Scythia was an ancient region in Eurasia; Leonardo uses it here to mean the far northern or eastern lands.</note> provinces will mix together in a great revolution.
<note>Leonardo is describing soil erosion and sedimentation. When heavy rains wash soil into rivers and then into the sea, the "earth" of one region is physically moved and deposited on the shores or seabed of another, effectively mixing the geography of different continents.</note>

### XXI. — THESE ARE THE RIVERS, WHICH CARRY AWAY THE EARTH STRIPPED BY THEM FROM THE MOUNTAINS, AND DEPOSIT IT UPON THE SEASHORES; AND WHERE THE EARTH ENTERS, THE SEA RETREATS.

The vast mountains, even though they are remote from the seashores, shall drive the sea from its place.
<note>Leonardo is describing the formation of deltas and the process of siltation. As rivers erode mountains and carry soil to the coast, the land expands into the ocean, "driving" the water away.</note>

### XXII. — OF THE WATER, WHICH RUNS TURBID AND MIXED WITH EARTH, AND OF THE DUST AND MIST MIXED WITH THE AIR, AND OF THE FIRE MIXED WITH ITS <note>original: "suo *", with a footnote indicating "elemento" (element) is implied.</note> ELEMENT AND OTHERS WITH EACH OTHER.

One will see all the elements mixed together in a great revolution, racing now toward the center of the world, now toward the sky; and at times from the southern regions rushing with fury toward the cold north, sometimes from the east toward the west, and thus from this to that other hemisphere.
<note>This "prophecy" describes the chaotic movement of matter during storms or geological shifts, where wind (air), rain (water), dust (earth), and lightning (fire) appear to lose their "natural" places and mix together.</note>

### XXIV. — OF THE NIGHT IN WHICH NO COLOR CAN BE RECOGNIZED.

It shall come to such a pass that no difference between colors will be known; instead, they will all become of a black quality.
<note>In this riddle, Leonardo describes how the absence of light (night) strips objects of their visible color, rendering everything uniform in darkness.</note>

### XXV. — OF FIRE.

There shall be born from a small beginning that which will quickly become great; this shall have no regard for any created thing, but rather by its power it will have the potential to transform almost everything from its own being into another.
<note>Leonardo refers to a spark that grows into a flame, consuming and transforming whatever it burns into ash, smoke, and heat.</note>

### XXVI. — THE CONCAVE MIRROR KINDLES THE FIRE WITH WHICH THE OVEN IS HEATED, WHICH HAS A BOTTOM LYING BENEATH ITS OWN SKY.

The solar rays shall kindle fire upon the earth, by which that which is under the sky shall be set aflame; and, having been reflected by its obstacle, they shall return downward.
<note>This describes the use of a "burning mirror" (a concave lens or mirror) to concentrate sunlight to start a fire. The "sky" of the oven refers to its vaulted ceiling.</note>

### XXVII. — TRACE.

Motion remains for us, which separates the mover from the moved.
<note>This brief note reflects Leonardo's studies into mechanics and the relationship between a force (the mover) and the object being acted upon (the moved).</note>

### XXVIII. — OF THE PLANETS.

And many terrestrial and aquatic animals shall mount among the stars: — that is, the planets.
<note>Leonardo refers to the zodiac and the constellations named after animals, such as Taurus (the bull), Cancer (the crab), or Pisces (the fish). By "mounting among the stars," he describes the naming of celestial bodies after creatures of the earth and sea.</note>

### XXIX. — OF COUNSEL.

And he who shall be most necessary to those in need of him, shall be unknown, that is, most despised.
<note>This riddle suggests that wise advice or the person offering it is often ignored or undervalued until the moment of crisis, or perhaps it refers to a humble tool that is overlooked until it becomes essential.</note>

### XXX. — OF THE FEAR OF POVERTY.

The evil and frightening thing shall cause such fear among men that, like madmen, believing they are fleeing from it, they shall run with swift motion into its boundless power.
<note>Leonardo observes the paradox of greed and anxiety: in their desperate attempt to escape poverty, people often engage in frantic labor or risky ventures that consume their lives and health, effectively falling into the very misery they sought to avoid.</note>

### XXXI. — OF THE LIE.

All things which in winter are hidden under the snow shall be uncovered and made manifest in the summer: — said of the lie, which cannot remain hidden.
<note>This is a moral metaphor using the change of seasons. Just as melting snow reveals what was buried beneath it, time inevitably reveals the truth, making the "winter" of a lie temporary.</note>

### I. — OF A FRIAR AND A MERCHANT.

The <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>Members of the Franciscan order, founded by St. Francis of Assisi, who took vows of poverty and traditionally lived on donations.</note> are accustomed, at certain times, to observe their particular <term>Lents</term> <note>Periods of fasting and abstinence from meat, modeled after the forty days before Easter.</note>, during which they do not eat meat within their convents; but when traveling, because they live on <term>alms</term> <note>Charitable donations, usually of food or money.</note>, they have permission to eat whatever is set before them. Thus, it happened that during these travels, a pair of such friars arrived at an inn in the company of a certain <term>petty merchant</term> <note>original: "mercantuolo." A diminutive term suggesting a merchant of small means or perhaps small character.</note>. They were seated at the same table, to which—due to the poverty of the inn—nothing was brought but a single roasted chicken. Whereupon the merchant, seeing that this was too little for himself alone, turned to the friars and said: "If I remember correctly, you do not eat meat of any kind in your convents on such days." At these words, the friars were compelled by their rule, without further <term>quibbling</term> <note>original: "cavillazioni." Sophistical or evasive arguments used to avoid a plain truth.</note>, to admit that this was the truth; wherefore the merchan-

When the merchant realized that the previous insult had been wittily avenged, he endured the vengeance with a pleasant laugh and peacefully, though half-blushing with shame.

## II. — CONCERNING A PAINTER AND A PRIEST.

While a priest was going through his <term>parish</term> <note>original: "parrocchia." A local church district under the care of a priest.</note> on <term>Holy Saturday</term> <note>The day before Easter, traditionally a time for priests to visit homes to bless them with holy water.</note>, giving <term>holy water</term> <note>original: "acqua benedetta." Water blessed by a priest for use in religious rituals.</note> throughout the houses as is the custom, he happened into the room of a painter. As he was sprinkling this water over some of his paintings, the painter turned around, somewhat annoyed, and asked why he was splashing such water over his pictures. Then the priest said that it was the custom and that it was his duty to do so, and that he was doing a good deed; and he who does good should expect good and even better, for so God promised, and that for every good deed done on earth, one would receive a hundredfold from above.

Then the painter, having waited for the priest to go outside, went up to the window and threw a large bucket of water onto the priest, saying: — "Look, here is the hundredfold coming to you from above, just as you said would happen for the good you did me with your holy water, with which you have ruined half my paintings!" —

### IV. — A CLEVER RESPONSE TO A PYTHAGOREAN.

A certain man, wishing to prove through the authority of **Pythagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher famous for his mathematical theorems and his belief in the "transmigration of souls," or reincarnation.</note> how he had lived in this world in a previous life, was being interrupted by another who would not let him finish his argument. So, the first man said to the other: — "As a sign that I have been here before, I remember that you were a **miller**." <note>original: "mulinaro."</note> — Then the other man, feeling the sting of these words, confirmed it was true, saying that by that same token he remembered that this fellow had been the **donkey** that used to carry the flour for him.

### VI. — A FRIEND TO A SLANDERER.

A certain man stopped associating with one of his friends because that friend often spoke ill of his other friends. This friend who had been left behind, meeting him one day and grieving deeply, begged him to say what the reason was that had made him forget such a great friendship. To him, the first man replied: — "I no longer wish to associate with you because I care for you; I do not want you to speak ill of me, your friend, to others, for then they would have to form a poor impression of you—just as I have—seeing you speak ill of me, who am your friend. Therefore, by us no longer spending time together, it will appear that we have become <term>enemies</term> <note>original: "nimici," an archaic form of "nemici."</note>, and when you speak ill of me, as is your habit, you will not be so blamed as you would be if we were still seen together." —

### VIII. — SAYING OF A SLEEPYHEAD.

It was said to a man that he should get out of bed because the sun had already risen, and he replied: — "If I had to travel as far and do as much business as he does, I too would already be up; however, having so little a journey to make, I do not want to get up yet." —

### IX. — A SHARP REMARK.

A man, seeing a woman prepared to <term>keep the table</term> <note>original: "tener tavola in giostra." This refers to a woman hosting a booth or serving as a prize/spectacle at a tournament or joust.</note> at a joust, looked at the target, and cried out upon seeing her lance: — "Alas! This is too small a worker for such a large shop!" — <note>In the ribald humor of the Renaissance, "shop" (bottega) and "worker" (lavorante) were common metaphors for sexual organs.</note>

### X. — RESPONSE TO A JEST.

Someone sees a large sword at the side of another man and says: — "Oh, you poor fellow! It is a great..."

### XI. — A WITTICISM DIRECTED AT A BRAGGART.

While one man was disputing and boasting of knowing how to perform many various and fine tricks, another among the bystanders said: — "I know how to do a trick that will make anyone I choose pull out their breeches <note>The joke relies on a pun on the verb "trarre," which can mean both "to pull off/remove" and "to pull out/produce."</note>." — The first braggart, knowing he was not wearing breeches <note>Men of this period often wore "calze" (joined hose) rather than separate "brache" (breeches/drawers).</note>, said: — "I bet you won't! I'll bet a pair of stockings on it." — The <term>proposer</term> <note>original: "pro-ponitore."</note> of the trick, having accepted the challenge, procured <note>original: "improntò." The author provides a synonym in the margin: "si procacciò."</note> several pairs of breeches and threw them into the face of the one who had staked the stockings, and thus he won the wager.

### XIII. — THE SAME.

### XIV. — A WITTICISM.

One man said that in his country the strangest things in the world were born. The other replied: — You, who were born there, confirm this to be true by the strangeness of your ugly presence. —

### XVI. — A WITTICISM.

<margin>5</margin>A man, going to Modena, had to pay 5 *soldi* of *Lira* <note>The lira and soldo were units of currency; 20 soldi made one lira.</note> as a tax on his person. At this, he began to make a great noise and show astonishment, attracting many bystanders. When they asked where such wonder came from, Maso replied: — Oh! Should I not wonder? Seeing that an entire man pays no more than 5 *soldi*, while in Florence I, just to put in my a[ss], had to pay 10 gold ducats <note>A massive sum compared to the 5 soldi mentioned earlier.</note>, and here I put in the a[ss], the b[alls], and all the rest for such a small tax. God save and maintain such a city, and those who govern it! — <note>Maso is likely joking about the heavy fines or taxes for "sodomy" or sexual misconduct in Florence compared to the cheap entry toll in Modena.</note>

### XVII. — A WITTY SAYING.

Two men were walking at night along a precarious path; the one in front made a great noise with his buttocks; and the other companion said: — Now I see that I am loved by you. — How so? said the other. — The first replied: — You offer me the <term>strap</term> <note>original: "coreggia." In Italian, this is a pun; it means both a leather strap (which one could hold onto in the dark) and a fart.</note>, so that I do not fall, nor lose my way from you. —

### XVIII. — A WITTY REMARK MADE BY A YOUNG MAN TO AN OLD MAN.

An old man was publicly scorning a young man, boldly showing that he did not fear him; wherefore the young man replied to him that his great age served him as a better shield than either his tongue or his strength. <note>The young man is cleverly insulting the elder; he suggests that the only reason he does not physically retaliate is because the man's frailty and age make him "off-limits" for a fight, not because the old man's arguments or power are intimidating.</note>

### XIX. — A WITTICISM.

Why the Hungarians have the double cross. <note>This refers to the "Patriarchal Cross" (a cross with two horizontal bars) which is a prominent symbol in Hungarian heraldry. Leonardo often recorded these prompts for jokes or symbolic fables, though the specific punchline or explanation is not provided in this entry.</note>

107 The source for information on **Pythagoras's** ideas regarding the <term>harmony of the spheres</term> <note>an ancient philosophical concept suggesting that the movements of celestial bodies create a celestial music that is usually inaudible to human ears</note> must be considered, in the final analysis, to be **Aristotle’s** *On the Heavens* <note>original: "De Cœlo"</note> (Book II, Chapter IX); nevertheless, Da Vinci proceeds independently of <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>refers to the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, named for the covered walkways where he taught</note> arguments. 110 The problem of the end of life in the

**111** According to **ANAXAGORAS** <note>a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC) who introduced the concept of "Nous" or Cosmic Mind</note>, everything in the world is composed of a sum of components of the same nature as the whole, which he himself called seeds <note>original: σπέρματα</note> (Fr. 1, 3, 6 [4]): these ultimate principles are found scattered everywhere, always equal to themselves, and enter into the composition of every inorganic and organic being. See **ZELLER**, *History of the Philosophy of the Greeks* <note>original: *Gesch. der Philosophie der Griechen*</note>. I, pages 875-885. The same expressions found in the fragment by **Leonardo** are also found in **BRUNO'S** *On the Shadows of Ideas* <note>original: *De umbris idearum*</note>, Berlin, 1868, page 28, and likely date back to **LUCRETIUS** <note>a Roman poet and philosopher known for his epic poem on Epicureanism</note>, *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: *De rerum natura*</note>, book I, line 830 and following.

**112** See: **ROBERTO VALTURIO** <note>an Italian engineer and author of a famous military treatise</note>, *On Military Matters* <note>original: *De re militari*</note>. Paris, 1534. Page 4, from which the fragment is taken.

**113** The information regarding these customs of savages was taken from **MANDEVILLE** <note>referring to the travels of Sir John Mandeville, a popular but largely fictionalized travel memoir of the 14th century</note>, *Treatise on the most marvelous and notable things found in the parts of the world* <note>original: *Tractato de le più maravigliose cosse e più notabili che si trovano in le parti del mondo*</note>. Milan, 1480, folio $l$ 4 recto:
> "and if they are fat they eat them at once, and if they are thin they make them fatten up."

The work by **PLATINA** <note>Bartolomeo Sacchi, known as Platina, was a Renaissance humanist and the first historian of the Papacy; he wrote a famous cookbook</note> cited here is *On honest pleasure and health and on victuals* <note>original: *De la honesta voluptate et valetudine et de li obsonij*</note>. Venice, 1487, recorded in the *Codex Atlanticus* with the words: *On honest pleasure* <note>original: *De onesta voluptà*</note>, folio 207 recto.

**114** The codex in which this fragment is found contains almost exclusively notes regarding the treatise **ON LIGHT AND SHADOW**. The horse mentioned here is the model for the equestrian statue of **Francesco Sforza** <note>the Duke of Milan; Leonardo worked for years on a massive bronze horse in his honor, which was never completed</note>.

**Jacomo Andrea**, in whose house Leonardo goes to dine with his pupil Giacomo, is **Andrea da Ferrara**, a profound connoisseur of **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect whose writings were the foundation of Renaissance architectural theory</note> and an architect of high renown, who died, killed by order of General **Trivulzio**, on May 15, 1500 (Compare G. Uzielli, *Research concerning Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: *Ricerche intorno a Leonardo da Vinci*</note>. Turin, 1896. Vol. I, pages 377-382). ***Marco*** is **Marco d'Oggionno**, a painter and disciple of da Vinci. ***Galeazzo Sanseverino***, in whose house Leonardo directed that tournament <note>a "giostra" or jousting event</note> which thereafter remained famous in Milan (January 26, 1491), is the captain to whom **Ludovico il Moro** <note>Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan and Leonardo’s primary patron</note> would entrust his army in the disastrous year of 1499, and a profound expert in the military arts. ***Agostino da Pavia*** is mentioned, together with Leonardo da Vinci, in the letter that **Bartolomeo Calco**, secretary to the **Sforza**, directed to the Referendary of Pavia on the occasion of the marriage of Ludovico to **Beatrice d'Este** and of **Anna** (sister of Duke Galeazzo) to **Alfonso d'Este**, to request the return of the artists who were in that city (December 8, 1490: ..... *Agostino and Master Leonardo*..... <note>original: "Augustino et Magistro Leonardo"</note>, compare Beltrami, *The Castle of Milan* <note>original: *Il Castello di Milano*</note>. Milan, 1895. Page 188). Finally, ***Gian Antonio*** is the artist **Gian Antonio Boltraffio**, another of Leonardo's disciples in Milan. This entire fragment is, almost without a doubt, a memorandum for the reimbursement of damages and expenses.

Page 228. One cannot deny, as **RICHTER** incautiously does (*The literary works of Leonardo da Vinci*. Vol. II, page 413), the possibility of such a custom existing among the inhabitants of the Indies, given the limited knowledge we possess of popular superstitious practices that lie beneath the higher principles of Asian religions. But it is more probable, and at the same time more natural, that Vinci refers—with the words: *as [is done] still in some region of India*—to the reports that were beginning to spread at the start of the 16th century in Europe regarding the customs of the American peoples <note>Leonardo often used "Indies" to refer to the Americas, as was common in the decades following Columbus's voyages</note>. If, on one hand, the **DIVISION OF THE BOOK** suggests the idea of a work of fiction <note>original: "narrazione fantastica"</note>, even if conducted with all the greater historical and geographical precision characteristic of Leonardo’s genius; there remains the need to explain the origin of certain reports; the reason for certain sketches—both rough and precise at the same time—which depict Asian men and objects; and the meaning of certain vague expressions regarding Oriental characters and customs that pop up unexpectedly in the manuscripts like memories of things seen, used as examples for principles of perspective or hydraulics. — 385. **Of the night in which no color is known.** <note>Leonardo often observed that darkness is the absence of all color, a fundamental principle in his theories on painting and optics.</note>
